'''Knowles:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Frank Murkowski]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Sarah Palin]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Alaska sidebar}} {{Sarah Palin series}} The '''2006 Alaska gubernatorial general election''' took place on November 7, 2006. Former [[Wasilla, Alaska|Wasilla]] mayor [[Sarah Palin]] defeated incumbent governor [[Frank Murkowski]] in the Republican primary, and then went on to defeat Democratic former governor [[Tony Knowles (politician)|Tony Knowles]] and independent [[Andrew Halcro]] in the general election. Palin became the first governor of the state to be born after Alaskan statehood. Palin would later become the unsuccessful Republican vice presidential nominee in the [[2008 United States presidential election]] before resigning as governor in 2009. == Republican primary == === Candidates === * [[John Binkley]], [[Fairbanks, Alaska|Fairbanks]] businessman and former State Senator from Bethel * [[2016 United States House of Representatives election in Alaska|Gerald Heikes]], minister at Anchorage's nondenominational Bethel Chapel and [[perennial candidate]] * Merica Hlatcu * [[Frank Murkowski]], incumbent Governor since 2003 * [[Sarah Palin]], former mayor of [[Wasilla, Alaska|Wasilla]] (1996{{Endash}}2003) and chair of the [[Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission]] (2003{{Endash}}04) Incumbent Frank Murkowski, first elected governor in 2002, ran for reelection but was defeated in a landslide in the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] primary by former Wasilla mayor [[Sarah Palin]] on August 22, 2006. Incumbent Republican Governor [[Bob Riley]] defeated Democratic Lieutenant Governor [[Lucy Baxley]]. Riley garnered 21% of [[African Americans]]' votes. Riley was the first Republican to carry the counties [[Bibb County, Alabama|Bibb]], [[Cherokee County, Alabama|Cherokee]], [[Etowah County, Alabama|Etowah]], [[Jackson County, Alabama|Jackson]], and [[Lauderdale County, Alabama|Lauderdale]] since Reconstruction. '''Hutchinson''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Mike Huckabee]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Mike Beebe]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsAR}} The '''2006 Arkansas gubernatorial election''' took place on Tuesday, November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Mike Huckabee]] was barred from seeking candidacy due to term limits set by the State Constitution in 1998, stating that the governor may only serve two terms in their lifetime. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] State Attorney General [[Mike Beebe]] defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] former U.S. representative [[Asa Hutchinson]] by a wide margin. This was the first open seat election since 1978. Hutchinson later served as Arkansas’ Governor from 2015 to 2023. == Democratic primary == === Nominee === * [[Mike Beebe]], [[Arkansas Attorney General]] == Republican primary == [[File:Asa Hutchinson campaigning.jpg|thumb|Hutchinson campaigning for governor in 2006]] === Candidates === *[[Asa Hutchinson]], former administrator of the [[Drug Enforcement Administration]], former [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representative]] from [[Arkansas's 3rd congressional district]] (1997–2001){{Cite web |last=Archives |first=L. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Janet Napolitano]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Janet Napolitano]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | image2 = File:Len Munsil.jpg | nominee2 = [[Len Munsil]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 543,528 | percentage2 = 35.44% | turnout = 60.47% {{increase}} 4.14pp {{Cite web|url=https://azsos.gov/elections/results-data/voter-registration-statistics|title=Voter Registration Statistics | Arizona Secretary of State|accessdate=7 May 2023}} }} {{Elections in Arizona sidebar}} The '''2006 Arizona gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent Governor Janet Napolitano was reelected in a landslide. Napolitano's widespread popularity contributed to her easy reelection; her general approval rating in October 2006, one month before the election, was at 58%.{{Cite web | url=http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2006/50StateGovernor061019State.htm |title = SurveyUSA {{pipe}} America's Neighborhood Pollster}} This was the last time until [[2022 Arizona gubernatorial election|2022]] that a Democrat was elected governor of Arizona. It is also the last time that a Democrat swept every county in the state in a statewide election. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== * [[Janet Napolitano]], incumbent [[governor of Arizona]] '''Angelides''': {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} | title = [[Governor of California|Governor]] | before_election = [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 32.77% {{decrease}}28.43pp }} {{ElectionsCA}} The '''2006 California gubernatorial election''' occurred in the US state on November 7, 2006. The [[Partisan primary|primary election]]s took place on June 6, 2006. The incumbent [[California Republican Party|Republican]] [[Governor of California|Governor]], [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]], won re-election for his first and only full term. His main opponent was [[California State Treasurer]] [[Phil Angelides]], the [[California Democratic Party]] nominee. [[Peter Camejo]] was the California [[Green Party of California|Green Party]] nominee, [[Janice Jordan]] was the [[Peace and Freedom Party (United States)|Peace and Freedom Party]] nominee, [[Art Olivier]] was the California [[Libertarian Party of California|Libertarian Party]] nominee, and [[Edward C. Noonan]] was the California [[American Independent Party]] nominee. Under the [[California Constitution|state constitution]], the [[Governor of California|governor]] serves a four-year term, with a maximum [[Term limits in the United States|term limit]] of two four-year terms for life, regardless of whether or not they are consecutive or nonconsecutive. [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] was elected in a [[2003 California recall|2003 recall election]] and served out the remainder of predecessor [[Gray Davis]]'s term ending in 2007; Schwarzenegger was therefore eligible to serve until 2011.{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/news/opinion/sunday/commentary/la-op-jeffe2jul02,0,1256025,print.story?coll=la-sunday-commentary|title=Think it can't get any wilder?|website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080619092345/http://www.latimes.com/news/opinion/sunday/commentary/la-op-jeffe2jul02%2C0%2C1256025%2Cprint.story?coll=la-sunday-commentary|archive-date=June 19, 2008|access-date=October 8, 2006}} As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this and the [[2006 California Insurance Commissioner election|concurrent Insurance Commissioner election]] mark the most recent time Republicans have won a statewide election in California, the most recent time a Republican was officially elected California governor, and the last election in which a California governor and lieutenant governor of opposite political parties were elected. Exit polls showed Schwarzenegger won the vote of [[White Americans|White]] (63%–32%) and [[Asian Americans]] (62%–37%), while Angelides won among [[African Americans]] (70%–27%) and [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Latinos]] (56%–39%).{{Cite web|date=November 2006|title=Exit Polls|url=https://www.cnn.com/ELECTION/2006/pages/results/states/CA/G/00/epolls.0.html|url-status=live|website=cnn.com|publisher=CNN}} == Primary election == Bar graph of statewide results{{cite web |url=http://primary2006.ss.ca.gov/Returns/gov/00.htm |title=CA Secretary of State – Primary Election- Governor of California – Statewide |publisher=Primary2006.ss.ca.gov |access-date=2010-08-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080828124126/http://primary2006.ss.ca.gov/Returns/gov/00.htm |archive-date=2008-08-28 |url-status=dead }} Results by county{{cite web |url=http://primary2006.ss.ca.gov/Returns/gov/00.htm#cty |title=CA Secretary of State – Primary Election- Governor of California – Statewide |publisher=Primary2006.ss.ca.gov |access-date=2010-08-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080828124126/http://primary2006.ss.ca.gov/Returns/gov/00.htm#cty |archive-date=2008-08-28 |url-status=dead }} The period for candidate nominations closed on March 24, 2006. === Republican === ==== Candidates ==== * Jeffrey Burns – general contractor * Bill Chambers – railroad switchman * Robert C. Newman II – psychologist and farmer * [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] – incumbent [[Governor of California]] Republican Schwarzenegger faced token opposition and won overwhelmingly in the primary held on June 6, 2006. ==== Results ==== {{Election box begin no change | title=Republican primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change| |party = California Republican Party |candidate = [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] (incumbent) |votes = 1,724,296 |percentage = 89.99% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = California Republican Party |candidate = [[Robert C. Newman II]] |votes = 68,663 |percentage = 3.58% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = California Republican Party |candidate = Bill Chambers |votes = 65,488 |percentage = 3.42% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = California Republican Party |candidate = [[Jeffrey R. Burns]] |votes = 57,652 |percentage = 3.01% }} {{Election box total no change| |votes = 1,916,099 |percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box end}} === Democratic === ==== Candidates ==== * [[Phil Angelides]] – [[California State Treasurer]]; former State Democratic Chair and developer * [[Barbara Becnel]] – Executive Director of Neighborhood House of North Richmond; founder of Save [[Stanley Tookie Williams]] campaign * Joe Brouilette – high school teacher * Edie Bukewihge – writer and publisher * Jerald Gerst – physician * Vibert Greene – engineer * Frank Macaluso – medical doctor * Michael Strimling – attorney * [[Steve Westly]] – [[California State Controller]]; former Internet executive The two front-runners for the Democratic nomination were Angelides and [[California State Controller]] [[Steve Westly]]. A pre-election poll had Westly leading Angelides by six percentage points.{{Cite web|date=April 2006|title=Special Survey on Education|url=https://www.ppic.org/content/pubs/survey/S_406MBS.pdf|url-status=live|website=ppic.org|publisher=Public Policy Institute of California|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060507222622/http://www.ppic.org/content/pubs/survey/S_406MBS.pdf |archive-date=2006-05-07 }} The Field Poll conducted on April 17, 2006, showed that both Democratic candidates had low recognition factors amongst the state's electorate, with only 45% having any opinion on Angelides and 40% for Westly. Of registered Democrats surveyed, 59% said they didn't know enough about Angelides to have any opinion about him, with 58% saying the same for Westly.{{cite web |url=http://field.com/fieldpollonline/subscribers/RLS2193.pdf |title=RLS2193 for PDF.PDF |access-date=2010-08-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101020150806/http://field.com/fieldpollonline/subscribers/RLS2193.pdf |archive-date=2010-10-20 |url-status=dead }} The ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' reported that the race for the Democratic nomination was a virtual tie, with Angelides leading Westly by three percentage points (37%–34%), within the 3% margin of error. Unusually, 28% of Democratic voters were undecided, and both candidates tried to earn the undecided vote. Angelides reported a recent increase in support for his campaign and gained union support as well as support from the "core" [[Liberalism in the United States|liberal]] constituency. The [[California Democratic Party]] endorsed him prior to the primary, despite most polls showing that Westly would fare much better against Schwarzenegger in the general election.{{Cite web|url=https://investortimes.com/progressreport/9269-2/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070509222636/http://www.californiaprogressreport.com/2006/04/angelides_endor.html|url-status=dead|title=Penny Wise Pound Foolish – Cuts in Free Flu Vaccines|first=Progress|last=Report|date=August 17, 2011|archivedate=May 9, 2007}} However, many registered Democrats believed that Westly had a greater chance of winning against incumbent governor Schwarzenegger and felt that he had a slightly "more positive" image.{{cite web |url=https://www.latimes.com/la-me-poll28may28,0,5948271.story?coll=la-story-footer |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20170525040730/http://articles.latimes.com/2006/may/28/local/me-poll28 |url-status=dead |archive-date=2017-05-25 |title=Angelides Pulls Even With Westly – Los Angeles Times |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=2006-05-28 |access-date=2010-08-14 }} In the end, Angelides won 47.9% of the vote to Westly's 43.4%. The turnout for the primary, was a record low 33.6%,{{cite web |url=http://primary2006.ss.ca.gov/Returns/status.htm |title=CA Secretary of State – Primary Election- County Status |publisher=Primary2006.ss.ca.gov |access-date=2010-08-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080828123746/http://primary2006.ss.ca.gov/Returns/status.htm |archive-date=2008-08-28 |url-status=dead }} far below the 38% predicted by the Secretary of State,{{Cite web|last=Demovic|first=Nghia Nguyen|date=2 June 2006|title=Secretary of State Bruce McPherson Predicts 38% Turnout for California Primary Election|url=http://www.ss.ca.gov/executive/press_releases/2006/06_078.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060628193518/http://www.ss.ca.gov/executive/press_releases/2006/06_078.pdf|archive-date=2006-06-28|website=ss.ca.gov}} with the turnout of valid ballots cast on election day at 28%.{{cite web|title=Gubernatorial Primary During his first two years, he came under fire from some conservatives for supporting several taxes on Californians,{{Cite news|last1=Halper|first1=Evan|last2=Rau|first2=Jordan|date=7 November 2008|title=Gov. pushes hike in sales tax, big cuts|work=Los Angeles Times|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2008-nov-07-me-arnold7-story.html|access-date=18 September 2020}} and from some [[American liberalism|liberals]] for refusing to sign a bill allowing [[Same-sex marriage in the United States|gay marriage]], and his support for several controversial propositions in 2005. {{collapse bottom}} ==Analysis== Results showed Schwarzenegger won 52 counties while Angelides won six; Schwarzenegger won an absolute majority in 48 counties and a plurality in four others, while Angelides won a majority in two counties and a plurality in four more. Schwarzenegger won large majorities in California's rural counties, the populous [[Southern California]] counties of [[San Diego County, California|San Diego]], [[Orange County, California|Orange]], [[Riverside County, California|Riverside]], [[San Bernardino County, California|San Bernardino]], and [[Ventura County, California|Ventura]], as well as populous [[Sacramento County, California|Sacramento]], [[Fresno County, California|Fresno]], and [[Kern County, California|Kern]] counties in the [[Central Valley (California)|Central Valley]]. The results were closely contested in [[Los Angeles County, California|Los Angeles County]] and in [[San Francisco Bay Area|Bay Area]] suburban counties. Angelides won substantially only in [[Alameda County, California|Alameda]] and [[San Francisco]] counties. [[Contra Costa County, California|Contra Costa]], [[Humboldt County, California|Humboldt]], [[Mendocino County, California|Mendocino]], [[Monterey County, California|Monterey]], [[Napa County, California|Napa]], [[Santa Clara County, California|Santa Clara]], [[Solano County, California|Solano]], [[Sonoma County, California|Sonoma]], and [[Yolo County, California|Yolo]] counties all voted for Schwarzenegger after voting No on the recall in 2003. == See also == * [[2006 United States gubernatorial elections]] * [[List of governors of California]] ==Notes== {{notelist}} == References == {{reflist|30em}} == External links == === Democratic candidates === * [https://web.archive.org/web/20061102110322/http://www.angelides.com// Phil Angelides] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060718031142/http://www.votebarbarabecnel-gov.com/ Barbara Becnel] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060615045241/http://www.voteedie.org/ Edie Bukewihge] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060502182648/http://www.westly2006.com/site/c.7nJGKPNrFqG/b.1021811/k.BCF8/Home.htm Steve Westly] === Republican candidates === * [https://web.archive.org/web/20061010092941/http://www.billchambers4governor.com/ Bill Chambers] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20061021002522/http://www.newman4governor.org/ Robert C. '''Beauprez''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Bill Owens (Colorado politician)|Bill Owens]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Bill Ritter]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsCO}} The '''2006 Colorado gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent Republican governor [[Bill Owens (Colorado politician)|Bill Owens]] was unable to run due to term limits, and the election was won by Democratic nominee [[Bill Ritter]]. With his win, Democrats obtained a trifecta in the state for the first time since 1963. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time the Governor's office in Colorado changed partisan control. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Bill Ritter]], former [[Denver District Attorney's Office|District Attorney of Denver]] ===Campaign=== In the leadup to the Democratic primary, [[Bill Ritter]], the former [[Denver District Attorney's Office|District Attorney of Denver]], emerged as the leading Democratic candidate. Though several other prominent state Democrats, including Denver Mayor [[John Hickenlooper]]{{cite news|date=February 6, 2006|title=Hickenlooper Won't Run for Governor|work=Summit Daily News|location=[[Breckenridge, Colorado]]|url=https://www.summitdaily.com/news/hickenlooper-wont-run-for-governor/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} and State House Speaker [[Andrew Romanoff]],{{cite news|date=January 4, 2006|title=Romanoff Passes on Governor's Race|work=Denver Business Journal|location=[[Denver, Colorado]]|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/denver/stories/2006/01/02/daily16.html|access-date=July 5, 2022}} considered running for Governor, both ultimately declined to do so. State Representative Gary Lindstrom, the only other candidate besides Ritter in the race, ended his campaign on February 28, 2006.{{cite news|date=February 28, 2006|title=Lindstrom Drops out of Governor's Race|work=[[Denver Post]]|location=[[Denver, Colorado]]|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2006/02/28/lindstrom-drops-out-of-governors-race-2/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} Ritter's personal opposition to abortion motivated pro-choice leaders in the state party to seek alternatives to him,{{cite news|date=April 15, 2006|title=Democrat Sidesteps the Abortion Plank|last=Riccardi|first=Nicholas|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|location=[[Los Angeles, California]]|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2006-apr-15-na-governor15-story.html|access-date=July 5, 2022}} but none ultimately materialized, and opposition to Ritter softened with his pledge to not alter the state's liberal abortion laws.{{cite news|date=February 14, 2006|title=Ritter Walks Tightrope with Abortion Stance|last=Crummy|first=Karen|work=[[Denver Post]]|location=[[Denver, percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== * [[Bob Beauprez]], U.S. Congressman from [[Colorado's 7th congressional district]] ===Campaign=== With popular two-term Governor [[Bill Owens (Colorado politician)|Bill Owens]] barred from seeking re-election, an open race developed for the Republican nomination to succeed him. The race looked like it would be between Congressman [[Bob Beauprez]], who represented the swingy Denver suburbs in Congress, and former [[University of Denver]] President [[Marc Holtzman]]. The race between Beauprez and Holtzman was contentious. Beauprez accused Holtzman of ethics violations, including making false allegations that the campaign's email list was stolen,{{cite news|date=June 22, 2006|title=Holtzman's Run is Done|last=Crummy|first=Karen|work=[[Denver Post]]|location=[[Denver, Colorado]]|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2006/06/22/holtzmans-run-is-done/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} providing falsified poll results to the ''[[Denver Post]]'', and using a separate state campaign committee as a "shadow gubernatorial campaign."{{cite news|date=May 1, 2006|title=Holtzman Calls Outside Probe Unnecessary|last=Crummy|first=Karen|work=[[Denver Post]]|location=[[Denver, Colorado]]|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2006/05/01/holtzman-calls-outside-probe-unnecessary/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} Holtzman, meanwhile, accused Beauprez of being part of the "politics of power" that he argued had taken the party away from its conservative values, pointing to Beauprez's support of Referendum C in 2005, which allowed the state to hold onto excess tax revenues rather than refund surpluses.{{cite news|date=January 6, 2006|title=Holtzman to GOP: 'Take Back the Party'|last=Roper|first=Peter|work=[[Pueblo Chieftain]]|location=[[Pueblo, Colorado]]|url=https://www.chieftain.com/story/news/2006/01/07/holtzman-to-gop-take-back/8432644007/|access-date=July 5, 2022}} In the end, the campaign between the two frontrunners fizzled. Beauprez won a landslide victory at the state Republican convention, denying Holtzman a spot on the ballot. Holtzman's efforts to collect signatures to win a spot on the ballot were ultimately in vain, with the [[Colorado Supreme Court]] ruling in June that he had failed to submit enough signatures. In response, Holtzman suspended his campaign and endorsed Beauprez, who won the Republican primary unopposed. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Bob Beauprez | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 193,804 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 193,804 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Campaign== === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- ! '''DeStefano:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Jodi Rell]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jodi Rell]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | image2 = Image:John DeStefano, Jr. in 2008 (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[John DeStefano Jr.]] | running_mate2 = Mary Glassman | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 398,220 | percentage2 = 35.45% }} {{ElectionsCT}} The '''2006 Connecticut gubernatorial election''' occurred on November 7, 2006. Incumbent Republican [[Jodi Rell]] became governor when [[John G. Rowland]] resigned on corruption charges in 2004. Rell had an approval rating of 70% as of October 19, 2006,{{cite web|url=http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2006/50StateGovernor061019State.htm |title=Approval Ratings for All 50 Governors |access-date=2006-11-05 |date=2006-10-19 |publisher=SurveyUSA}} and polls showed her leading the Democratic nominee, New Haven mayor [[John DeStefano Jr.|John DeStefano]] by a near 30-point margin. As expected, she won the election to a full term in a landslide. DeStefano defeated Stamford Mayor [[Dannel Malloy]] in the Connecticut Democratic gubernatorial primary on August 8. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time a Republican and woman was elected Governor of Connecticut, and the last time any gubernatorial candidate won [[List of counties in Connecticut|every 2006 Florida gubernatorial election.text:

'''Davis''': {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Jeb Bush]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Charlie Crist]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | turnout = 46.8%{{decrease}}8.5{{cite web |url=https://results.elections.myflorida.com/Index.asp?ElectionDate=11/7/2006&DATAMODE=|title=November 7, 2006 General Election|website=Florida Department of State|access-date=2022-05-15}} }} {{ElectionsFL}} The '''2006 Florida gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006. Incumbent Republican Governor [[Jeb Bush]] was [[term-limited]], and could not run for election to a third consecutive term. The election was won by then-Republican [[Charlie Crist]], the state's attorney general. The election was notable in that for the first time, the state elected a Republican governor in three consecutive elections. Turnout for the 2006 election was down 8.5% from 2002 and down 2.7% from 1998.{{Cite web |url=http://election.dos.state.fl.us/elections/resultsarchive/Index.asp |title=Florida Department of State – Division of Elections (Election Results) |access-date=2014-10-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150218074840/http://election.dos.state.fl.us/elections/resultsarchive/index.asp |archive-date=2015-02-18 |url-status=dead }} With Republicans holding the seat, the state's governorship avoided being part of the [[United States elections, 2006|wave]] in which Democrats netted a gain of six governorships across the nation.{{cite news|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/democrats-retake-majority-of-governorships/|title=Democrats Retake Majority Of Governorships|work=CBS News|first=Amy|last=Clark|date=November 8, 2006|access-date=October 23, 2014}} This remains the last time that Charlie Crist won a statewide election in Florida, as well as the last election in which he ran as a Republican. This was the last time until [[2022 Florida gubernatorial election|2022]] that anyone was elected governor with a majority of the vote. To date, this is the last time Florida simultaneously elected a United States Senate candidate and a gubernatorial candidate of different political parties. ==Democratic primary== ===Campaign=== [[Jim Davis (Florida politician)|Jim Davis]] won the Democratic primary on September 5. Davis was the [[congressman]] from [[Florida's 11th congressional district]] and served in the [[Florida House of Representatives]], where he also served as the majority leader. On September 13, Davis selected former state senator and 2002 gubernatorial candidate [[Daryl Jones (politician)|Daryl Jones]] of [[Miami]] as his running mate. The Democratic primary turned heated as it approached primary day. [[Rod Smith (politician)|Rod Smith]] attacked [[Jim Davis (Florida politician)|Jim Davis]] for a 1990 legislative vote denying restitution for two black men wrongfully imprisoned for murder. Davis countered that Smith was a "pawn" of the sugar industry, and that "[[big business]]" and [[Advocacy group|special interests]] were funding many of Smith's attack ads. ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== *Glenn Burkett *Carol Castagnero, retired teacher *John M. Previously he was elected State Education Commissioner, and has served in the [[Florida Senate]]. He faced [[Bob Graham]] for his seat in the [[United States Senate]] in 1998. On September 13, 2006, Crist announced that State Representative [[Jeff Kottkamp]] of [[Cape Coral]] would be his running mate. The GOP primary did not end up being very competitive. Crist touted experience in statewide offices, and a strong fundraising capability. He portrayed himself as relatively moderate on social issues, which created some misgivings among conservative Republicans in the state, but not nearly enough to sway the vote to [[Tom Gallagher]].{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/09/04/us/04florida.html?_r=0|title=In Days Before Primary, Hackles Start Rising in Race for Florida Governor|work=The New York Times|first=Abby|last=Goodnough|date=September 6, 2006|access-date=October 23, 2014}} ===Candidates=== ====Declared==== *[[Charlie Crist]], [[attorney general of Florida]], and nominee for [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] in [[1998 United States Senate election in Florida|1998]] *[[Tom Gallagher]], [[chief financial officer of Florida]], former State Treasurer-Insurance Commissioner, former Education Commissioner, and candidate for governor in [[Florida gubernatorial election, 1986|1986]] and [[Florida gubernatorial election, 1994|1994]] *Vernon Palmer *Michael W. |} ==Results== Charlie Crist won by over 7 points, winning all Republican-leaning areas of Florida, as well as the notable "swing" region along the I-4 corridor (Daytona Beach, Orlando, Tampa/St. Petersburg). Davis performed well in the Democrat-leaning south Florida, Gainesville, and Tallahassee areas. Crist under-performed compared to his predecessor [[Jeb Bush]], but still outpaced Davis, despite the low turnout. [[Reform Party of the United States of America|Reform Party]] candidate Max Linn received nearly 2% of the vote, but his sizeable haul of over 92,500 votes was still not enough to sway the election. Crist also won 18% of the African-American electorate, which outpaced previous Republicans' efforts in attracting this voting bloc in statewide elections. Also on the ballot the same day was a [[Constitution of Florida|constitutional]] amendment to raise the requirement for all future ballot initiatives to a supermajority (60%). Previously, constitutional amendments put on the ballot required only a simple majority (50% +1) to be approved, and led to some controversial amendments being put on the ballot. Support and opposition for the amendment fell loosely along party lines with Democrats generally opposing its passage. Both Crist and Davis publicly opposed the measure,{{Cite web |url=http://www.flaflcio.org/sites/default/files/11-solidarity/11_October-November_2006.pdf |title=Solidarity |access-date=2016-11-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170326102749/http://www.flaflcio.org/sites/default/files/11-solidarity/11_October-November_2006.pdf |archive-date=2017-03-26 |url-status=dead }} but it was passed anyway by the voters with a 55% margin - a higher margin than either candidate received. {{Election box begin | title=2006 Florida gubernatorial election{{cite web|url=https://results.elections.myflorida.com/DetailRpt.Asp?ELECTIONDATE=11/7/2006&RACE=GOV&PARTY=&DIST=&GRP=&DATAMODE=|title=November 7, 2006 General Election, Governor and Lieutenant Governor|publisher=Florida Department of State Division of Elections| access-date=June 30, 2016}}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link| |party = Republican Party (United States) |candidate = [[Charlie Crist]]/[[Jeff Kottkamp]] |votes = 2,519,845 |percentage = 52.20% |change = -3.81% }} {{Election box candidate with party link| |party = Democratic Party (United States) |candidate = [[Jim Davis (Florida politician)|Jim Davis]]/[[Daryl Jones (politician)|Daryl Jones]] |votes = 2,178,289 |percentage = 45.10% |change = +1.94% }} {{Election box candidate with party link| |party = Reform Party (United States) |candidate = Max Linn |votes = 92,595 |percentage = 1.90% |change = +1.90% }} {{Election box candidate with party link| |party = Independent (politician) |candidate = John Wayne Smith |votes = 15,987 |percentage = 0.30% |change = }} {{Election box candidate with party link| |party = Independent (politician) |candidate = Richard Paul Dembinsky |votes = 11,921 |percentage = 0.20% |change = }} {{Election box candidate with party link| |party = Independent (politician) |candidate = Karl C.C. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Sonny Perdue]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Sonny Perdue]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsGA}} The '''2006 Georgia gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Sonny Perdue]] ran for re-election to a second and final term as governor. Governor Perdue was renominated by the Republican Party, defeating a minor opponent in the process, while Lieutenant Governor [[Mark Taylor (American politician)|Mark Taylor]] narrowly emerged victorious from a competitive [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] primary. In the general election, though Taylor ran a spirited campaign, Perdue was aided by the increasing tendency of the state to vote for Republicans and by his popularity with the public; polling showed his approval ratings above sixty percent. In the end, Perdue was overwhelmingly re-elected as governor, defeating Taylor in a [[Landslide victory|landslide]], becoming the first Republican governor of Georgia to ever be reelected. {{As of|2024}}, this is the last time that [[Muscogee County, Georgia|Muscogee]], [[Warren County, Georgia|Warren]], [[Rockdale County, Georgia|Rockdale]], [[Chatham County, Georgia|Chatham]], and [[Bibb County, Georgia|Bibb]] counties voted for the Republican candidate for governor and the last time that [[Marion County, Georgia|Marion]], [[Telfair County, Georgia|Telfair]], and [[Wheeler County, Georgia|Wheeler]] counties voted for the Democratic candidate.{{Citation needed|date=January 2025}} Exit polls showed that Perdue won white voters (68% to 27%) while Taylor won black voters (81% to 17%). As of 2025, Perdue's 17% of the African American vote is the highest showing of any Republican seeking statewide office in Georgia.{{Citation needed|date=January 2025}} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== * Bill Bolton * [[Cathy Cox (American politician)|Cathy Cox]], [[Secretary of State of Georgia]] * Mac McCarley * [[Mark Taylor (American politician)|Mark Taylor]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Georgia]] ===Results=== [[File:06GAGubDemCounties.PNG|thumb|right|180px|2006 Georgia Democratic gubernatorial primary. Dark blue indicates Taylor, while light blue indicates Cox.]] {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results{{cite web |title=Georgia Election Results Official Results of the July 18, 2006 Primary Election |url=http://sos.georgia.gov/elections/election_results/2006_0718/summary.htm |website=sos.georgia.gov |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080206211010/http://sos.georgia.gov/elections/election_results/2006_0718/summary.htm |archive-date=6 February 2008 |url-status=dead}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Mark Taylor | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 249,188 | percentage = 52.1% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Cathy Cox | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 211,978 | percentage = 44.3% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Bill Bolton | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 10,552 | percentage = 1.7% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Mac McCarley | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 10,399 | percentage = 0.6% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 482,117 | percentage= 100 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== * Ray McBerry, businessman * [[Sonny Perdue]], incumbent [[governor of Georgia]] ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Sonny Perdue (incumbent) | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 370,756 | percentage = 88.4% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Ray McBerry | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 48,498 | percentage = 12.6% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 419,254 | percentage= 100 }} {{Election box end}} ==General election== ===Fundraising=== Perdue had more financial resources on hand than Taylor. As of the March 31 filing, Perdue reported that he had over $8.2 million on hand,{{Cite web |title=Campaign Reports Search {{!}} Georgia Government Campaign Finance Commission of Georgia |url=https://media.ethics.ga.gov/search/Campaign/Campaign_Name.aspx?NameID=293&FilerID=C2006000088&Type=candidate |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=media.ethics.ga.gov}} while Taylor had $4.2 million in reserve.{{Cite web |title=Campaign Reports Search {{!}} Georgia Government Campaign Finance Commission of Georgia |url=https://media.ethics.ga.gov/search/Campaign/Campaign_ReportOptions.aspx?NameID=291&FilerID=C2006000087&CDRID=4217 |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=media.ethics.ga.gov}} Perdue had the added advantage of facing a weak opponent in Ray McBerry in the primary election, while Cox and Taylor engaged in a bitter struggle for the Democratic nomination. Garrett Hayes, the Libertarian candidate, reported less than $1,000 on hand,{{Cite web |title=Campaign Reports Search {{!}} Georgia Government Campaign Finance Commission of Georgia |url=https://media.ethics.ga.gov/search/Campaign/Campaign_Name.aspx?NameID=295&FilerID=C2006000089&Type=candidate |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=media.ethics.ga.gov}} though the October 31 Zogby poll showed him attracting a surprising 9.1 percent of polled voters.{{Cite web |last=Doherty |first=Brian |date=2006-11-08 |title=And the Georgia Gubernatorial Race and the Libertarian Party? |url=https://reason.com/2006/11/07/and-the-georgia-gubernatorial/ |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=Reason.com |language=en-US}} ===Advertisements=== A minor controversy developed during the primary campaign over an ad created by Georgians for Truth, a group founded by several prominent Democratic fundraisers. The ad criticized Perdue for allegedly failing to pay his taxes for several years before becoming governor, allegations that had been made in the 2002 campaign as well. Cox and Taylor, for reasons that are not clear, requested that the group not run the ad, prompting the [[Georgia Democratic Party]] chairman, Bobby Kahn, to strongly rebuke the group's members.{{Cite web |author=Staff Writer |title=Flagger runs in GOP primary against Perdue |url=https://www.savannahnow.com/story/news/2006/04/19/flagger-runs-in-gop-primary/13753070007/ |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=Savannah Morning News |language=en-US}} === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- ! Source ! Ranking ! As of |- | align=left | [[The Cook Political Report]]{{Cite web|title=2006 Governor Race Ratings for November 6, 2006|url=https://cookpolitical.com/races/report_pdfs/2006_gov_ratings_nov6.pdf|website=The Cook Political Report|access-date=October 1, 2006|archive-date=June 5, 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080605094803/https://cookpolitical.com/races/report_pdfs/2006_gov_ratings_nov6.pdf|url-status=dead}} | {{USRaceRating|Lean|R}} | November 6, 2006 |- | align=left | [[Sabato's Crystal Ball]]{{cite web | title=Election Eve 2006: The Final Predictions | url=https://centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/articles/ljs2006110601/ | website=Sabato's Crystal Ball | access-date=June 25, 2021}} | {{USRaceRating|Safe|R}} | November 6, 2006 |- | align=left | [[Stuart Rothenberg|Rothenberg Political Report]]{{cite web | title=2006 Gubernatorial Ratings | url=https://www.insideelections.com/ratings/governor/2006-gubernatorial-ratings | work=Senate Ratings | publisher=The Rothenberg Political Report | access-date=June 25, 2021}} | {{USRaceRating|Safe|R}} | November 2, 2006 |- | align=left | [[Real Clear Politics]]{{cite web | title=Election 2006 | url=https://www.realclearpolitics.com/epolls/writeup/election_2006-21.html| publisher=Real Clear Politics | access-date=June 25, 2021}} | {{USRaceRating|Likely|R}} | November 6, 2006 |} ===Campaign issues=== ====Education==== * ''The [[HOPE Scholarship]]'' program and its stability and continued solvency are recurring issues in Georgia politics. Citing budget constraints, Perdue signed Republican-sponsored legislation that significantly cut the benefits conferred by the program. Cox and Taylor both severely criticized the governor for these actions, and both pointed to the fact that Perdue voted against the legislation creating the program as a state senator in 1993. Perdue backed an amendment to the [[Georgia (U.S. state) Constitution|state constitution]] that would have shifted the allocation of the lottery funds that support the program, but the legislation was defeated.{{Cite web |last=Larrabee |first=Brandon |title=Restrictions up fees for HOPE scholars |url=https://www.savannahnow.com/story/news/2006/08/16/restrictions-fees-hope-scholars/13829762007/ |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=Savannah Morning News |language=en-US}} ::On April 19, 2006, Cox charged that Taylor had not sponsored the HOPE scholarship legislation in 1993, as he claimed. Taylor apparently sponsored a companion bill that did not pass, although he supported the bill that did pass. The incident portended a strongly negative campaign for the Democratic nomination. * ''College tuition'' may also be an issue. During Perdue's first term, Georgia's universities substantially increased tuition fees. * ''School funding'': Perdue successfully backed legislation that requires Georgia schools to spend at least 65% of their budgets "in the classroom". Democrats charged that some school programs, such as music classes, do not fit the definition of "in the classroom." ====Health care==== * ''[[PeachCare]]'', a state program providing medical care for needy children and families, emerged as a point of contention between Perdue and his challengers. Perdue approved a cut in the program during his administration. Taylor, a strong supporter of the program, was particularly vocal in attacking Perdue and advocating significant expansion of the program.{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Walter C. |title=Perdue, Taylor see health care differently |url=https://www.savannahnow.com/story/news/2006/09/18/perdue-taylor-see-health-care-differently/13826599007/ |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=Savannah Morning News |language=en-US}} * Perdue made [[Medicaid]] reform a priority during his first term. Democrats were critical of the reform proposal that Perdue presented to federal officials. ====Immigration==== The problem presented by illegal immigrants emerged during Georgia's 2006 legislative session as an issue likely to have a large impact on the gubernatorial campaign. Perdue signed legislation restricting the ability of illegal immigrants to access state resources, including health care and public education.{{Cite web |author=Staff Writer |title=Perdue signs controversial bill |url=https://www.augustachronicle.com/story/news/2006/04/18/met-77913-shtml/14770221007/ |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=The Augusta Chronicle |language=en-US}} ====Voting==== * ''Voter identification'' legislation signed by Perdue requiring photo identification for voting while expanding absentee voting opportunities had a substantial impact on the campaign. Democrats strongly denounced the legislation as discriminatory against the poor and elderly, while Republicans attempted to alleviate such concerns by providing access to photo identification for those not possessing it.{{Cite web |last=Gross |first=Doug |title=Governor signs voter ID measure |url=https://www.augustachronicle.com/story/news/2006/01/27/met-49863-shtml/14777315007/ |access-date=2024-10-18 |website=The Augusta Chronicle |language=en-US}} * ''Paper ballots'' were a major concern of Taylor supporters, who felt that Cox made a mistake when she brought electronic '''Lingle''': {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Linda Lingle]] | after_election = [[Linda Lingle]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsHI}} The '''2006 Hawaii gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Linda Lingle]] was the first Republican to be elected governor of Hawaii since [[1959 Hawaii gubernatorial election|1959]]. Although [[2006 United States elections|2006]] was a strong election year for Democrats, Lingle won re-election by a landslide owing to an economic rebound in the state that occurred during her tenure after a shaky decade for the state economy during the 1990s and early 2000s. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the last time a Republican won a statewide election in Hawaii, as well as the only time in Hawaii history that a Republican governor was re-elected. Additionally, this alongside [[1972 United States presidential election in Hawaii|1972 United States presidential election]] were the only two times Republicans won the state with more than 60% of the vote. == Republican primary == === Candidates === * [[Linda Lingle]], incumbent governor * George L. '''Nussle:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#c21b18|80–90%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Tom Vilsack]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Chet Culver]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsIA}} The '''2006 Iowa gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006. The incumbent [[List of governors of Iowa|governor]], [[Tom Vilsack]], a [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]], had served two terms and decided not to seek a third. In the election, [[Chet Culver]] defeated [[Jim Nussle]] to win the governorship, by a margin of 54% to 44%.{{cite news |last=Beaumont |first=Thomas |title=Culver sails into victory |publisher=[[Des Moines Register]] |date=November 8, 2006 |url=http://www.dmregister.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20061108/NEWS09/311080011|access-date=2006-11-09}} This election marks the first time Democrats won three consecutive gubernatorial elections in the state since [[1966 Iowa gubernatorial election|1966]], and the only time Democrats have ever done so for four-year terms. Until [[Rob Sand|Rob Sand’s]] win in [[2026 Iowa gubernatorial election|2026]], this was the last time a Democrat was elected Governor of Iowa. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== ==== Won primary '''Topinka:''' {{legend0|#ffc8cd|30–40%}} {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Rod Blagojevich]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Rod Blagojevich]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | turnout = 47.29% {{decrease}} 2.76 [[Percentage point|pp]] }} {{ElectionsIL}} The '''2006 Illinois gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Governor of Illinois|Governor]] [[Rod Blagojevich]] won re-election to a second four-year term scheduled to have ended on January 10, 2011. However, Blagojevich did not complete his term, as he was impeached and removed from office in 2009. This was the first election since [[1964 Illinois gubernatorial election|1964]] that a Democrat was re-elected governor. Many observers expected the race to be close, especially considering the [[opinion poll|polling]],{{cite web|url=http://www.surveyusa.com/client/PollReport.aspx?g=8eca95c7-104b-43c0-8ca5-20048b49913a |title=SurveyUSA News Poll #8260 |publisher=Surveyusa.com |access-date=2015-03-30}} which had shown Governor Blagojevich to have a high disapproval rating. However, the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]]s had fared poorly due to scandals involving prior Governor [[George Ryan]], and the increasingly unpopular presidency of [[George W. Bush]]. Exit polls showed Topinka won white voters (46%–41%-13%), while Blagojevich performed well among African Americans (80%–16%-2%) and Latinos (83%–12%-4%). Democrats won Will County for the first time since 1964, and Lake County for the first time since 1960. This was the second and last time in Illinois that a woman was a major party's nominee for governor, the other being [[1994 Illinois gubernatorial election|1994]]. ==Background== The primaries and general elections coincided with those for [[2006 United States House of Representatives elections in Illinois|Congress]] and those for other state offices. The election was part of the [[2006 Illinois elections]]. {{See also|2006 Illinois elections#Turnout}} For the primaries, turnout for the gubernatorial primaries was 23.13%, with 1,680,207 votes cast and turnout for the lieutenant gubernatorial primaries was 20.60% with 1,496,453 votes cast.{{cite web |title=Voter Turnout |url=https://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionOperations/VoterTurnout.aspx Schadow | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 17 | percentage = 0.00 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 819,022 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== ===Governor=== ====Candidates==== * [[Bill Brady (politician)|Bill Brady]], [[Illinois State Senate|Illinois state Senator]] * [[Ronald Gidwitz|Ron Gidwitz]], businessman and former chairman of the [[Illinois State Board of Education]] * [[Andy Martin]], perennial candidate * [[Jim Oberweis]], owner of [[Oberweis Dairy]] * [[Judy Baar Topinka]], [[Illinois state treasurer]] ====Declined==== * [[Jim Edgar]], former governor{{cite web | url=https://news.stlpublicradio.org/other/2005-09-30/jim-edgar-says-no-to-run-for-illinois-governor | title=Jim Edgar says no to run for Illinois Governor | date=30 September 2005 }} ====Campaign==== On November 7, 2005, Topinka announced that she would not seek re-election as state treasurer — instead, she entered the gubernatorial primary, hoping to challenge Democratic Governor [[Rod Blagojevich]]. The Republican primary was deeply divisive; her tenure as party chairman destroyed her support from the conservative wing of her party, and it was feared that her [[pro-choice]] and positive [[gay rights]] positions would be detrimental to her standing with the same conservatives. In December she announced that she would join forces with [[DuPage County]] State's Attorney [[Joe Birkett]] as a candidate for lieutenant governor of Illinois. In February 2006, the candidates for the Republican nomination for Illinois governor began running their first TV ads for the March statewide primary election. Rival candidate [[Ronald Gidwitz|Ron Gidwitz]]'s advertisements attacking Topinka were rebuked in the same week by the Illinois Republican Party: "In an unprecedented action, the Illinois Republican Party has officially rebuked the Gidwitz campaign for this ad because the Party found that the ad violates the Party's "Code of Conduct", which was enacted to police proper conduct among Republican candidates." Later in February, candidate [[James D. Oberweis|Jim Oberweis]], another rival for the Republican gubernatorial nomination, started a series of attack ads for television markets, against Topinka, that were even more widely criticized, mostly for using "fake" headlines on the images of actual Illinois newspapers.{{Ref|Tribune}}{{Ref|FactCheck}} These ads, like Gidwitz's ads, also came under review by the Illinois Republican Party.{{Ref|SLPD}} Because of the controversy generated, several television stations withdrew Oberweis's ads.{{Ref|DH}} ====Results==== [[File:2006 Illinois gubernatorial Republican primary results Party]] became an established political party statewide, according to Illinois state election law, when Rich Whitney received more than 5% of the total vote for governor. The new status provided the party with several new advantages, such as lower signature requirements for ballot access, primary elections, free access to additional voter data, the ability to elect precinct committeemen, run a partial slate of candidates at any jurisdictional level, and ''slate'' candidates without petitioning. The only other statewide established political parties were the [[Democratic Party of Illinois|Democratic]] and [[Illinois Republican Party|Republican]] parties. It is rare for a new political party to become established statewide in Illinois, the last to do so being the [[Solidarity Party (Illinois)|Solidarity Party]] in 1986 and the [[Progressive Party (United States, 1912)|Progressive Party]] before that. ==See also== * [[2006 Illinois elections]] * [[2006 United States gubernatorial elections]] * [[2006 United States House of Representatives elections in Illinois]] ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== '''Official campaign websites (archived)''' * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060208225125/http://www.whitneyforgov.org/ Whitney's campaign website] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20061030111515/http://www.rodforillinois.com/ Blagojevich's campaign website] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20061025192044/http://www.judyforgov.com/ Topinka's campaign website] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060423015511/http://www.runrandyrun.com/ Stufflebeam's campaign website] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20070305061314/http://www.markmccoy.com/ Mark McCoy's campaign website] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060619031907/http://kochforgovernor.com/ Koch's campaign website] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060404182926/http://www.standingupforillinois.org/ Quinn's campaign website] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060220093058/http://www.joebirkett.com/ Birkett's campaign website] {{2006 U.S. midterm elections}} {{US Third Party Election}} {{Rod Blagojevich}} {{Illinois elections}} [[Category:2006 elections in Illinois|Governor]] [[Category:Illinois gubernatorial elections|2006]] [[Category:2006 United States gubernatorial elections|Illinois]] [[Category:Rod Blagojevich]]

Incumbent Democratic Governor [[Kathleen Sebelius]], who sported high approval ratings{{Cite web| title=Approval Ratings For All 50 Governors| url=http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2006/50StateGovernor060720State.htm| publisher=SurveyUSA/KWCH-TV/KCTV-TV| date=2006-07-20| access-date=2007-11-28}} ran for re-election to serve a second and final term. She was unopposed for the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nomination and faced [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Kansas State Senate|State Senator]] [[Jim Barnett (Kansas politician)|Jim Barnett]], who emerged from a crowded primary. Sebelius defeated Barnett and was re-elected with more than 57% of the vote. Barnett ran for Governor of Kansas again in 2018 and lost the Republican primary. Sullivan]] | popular_vote3 = 154,628 | percentage3 = 6.89% }} {{ElectionsMA}} The '''2006 Massachusetts gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. The incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor, [[Mitt Romney]], chose not to seek a second term. Polls had been mixed prior to Romney's announcement, with one poll showing Romney slightly leading [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Attorney General of Massachusetts|Attorney General]] [[Thomas Reilly (Massachusetts politician)|Tom Reilly]] and other polls showing Reilly, who was then the Democratic frontrunner, in the lead.[http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2005/11/17/poll_shows_romney_gaining_on_reilly_reilly_leading_healey Polls show Romney gaining on Reilly, Reilly leading Healey]{{dead link|date=May 2026|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} ''Boston Globe'' November 17, 2005 The election was won by the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] former United States Assistant Attorney General [[Deval Patrick]], who became the second African-American governor in the United States since [[Reconstruction Era|Reconstruction]] and the first Democratic governor of Massachusetts since [[Michael Dukakis]] left office in 1991. This was the last time until [[2022 Massachusetts gubernatorial election|2022]] that the Democratic nominee won a majority. Healey is the only Republican gubernatorial nominee never to be elected governor between 1990 and 2018. ==Republican primary== ===Governor=== ====Candidates==== * [[Kerry Healey]], lieutenant governor of Massachusetts =====Declined===== * [[Christy Mihos]], businessman (running as an independent) * [[Mitt Romney]], incumbent governor ''(endorsed Healey)'' Healey was unopposed for the Republican nomination. ===Lieutenant governor=== ====Candidates==== * Reed Hillman, former state representative and Massachusetts State Police colonel As incumbent Kerry Healey ran for governor, the position of lieutenant governor was open. Reed Hillman was unopposed for the Republican nomination. ==Democratic primary== ===Governor=== ====Candidates==== * [[Chris Gabrieli]], businessman and lieutenant governor nominee in [[Massachusetts gubernatorial election, 2002|2002]][https://archive.boston.com/news/local/articles/2006/03/22/gabrieli_readies_run_for_governor/ Gabrieli readies run for governor] ''Boston Globe'' March 22, 2006 * [[Deval Patrick]], former [[United States Assistant Attorney General|assistant U.S. attorney general]] for [[United States Department of Justice Civil Rights Division|Civil Rights]] * [[Thomas Reilly (Massachusetts politician)|Thomas Reilly]], [[Attorney General of Massachusetts|Massachusetts attorney general]] ====Endorsements==== * Deval Patrick: ''[[Attleboro Sun Chronicle]]'', ''[[Bay State Banner]]'', ''[[Blue Mass Group]]'', ''[[Boston Globe]]'', ''[[Brookline TAB|Brookline Tab]]'', ''[[Cambridge Chronicle]]'', ''[[Hamilton-Wenham Chronicle]]'', ''[[Wellesley Townsman]]'', ''[[Worcester Magazine]]'' * Tom Reilly: ''[[Boston Herald]]'', ''[[Cape Cod Times]]'', ''[[Springfield Republican]]'' ====Campaign==== The Democratic state caucuses were held in February in all cities and towns to elect delegates to the state convention. The Patrick campaign organized their supporters, many of whom had never been involved in such party processes before, to win twice as many pledged delegates as the Reilly campaign. (Chris Gabrieli did not join the race until a month later, which played a major role in his difficulty in getting on the ballot.) At the Democratic Convention on June 3 in Worcester, each candidate needed to receive support from 15% of the delegates to be on the primary ballot in September. There was some question as to whether Gabrieli could succeed after entering the race so late. Patrick received the convention's endorsement with 57.98% of the vote, Reilly made it with 26.66%, and Gabrieli narrowly achieved ballot access with 15.36% of the delegates' votes.[http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2006/06/03/reilly_proclaims_success_in_reaching_democratic_ballot Patrick garners most votes; Reilly touts success at convention] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060614114639/http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2006/06/03/reilly_proclaims_success_in_reaching_democratic_ballot/ |date=June 14, 2006 }} ''Boston Globe'' June 3, 2006[http://www.boston.com/news/local/politics/blog/2006/06/all_candidates_1.html All candidates make it..] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060614053240/http://www.boston.com/news/local/politics/blog/2006/06/all_candidates_1.html |date=June 14, 2006 }} ''Boston Globe'' June 3, 2006 The campaign was highlighted by numerous debates. Deval Patrick followed with his acceptance speech, appearing with his new running mate Tim Murray and former opponent Chris Gabrieli. The general election campaign was very heated and was referred to by [[Michael Dukakis]] as "the dirtiest gubernatorial campaign in my memory".[https://archive.boston.com/news/globe/ideas/articles/2006/10/29/enough/ Enough ''by Mike Dukakis''] ''The Boston Globe'', October 29, 2006 The Healey campaign released attack ads implying that Deval Patrick supports sexual assault or murder of police (culminating in the now infamous "parking lot rape" ad). Healey supporters also protested at the homes of Patrick and Patrick campaign manager [[John E. Walsh]],{{Cite web |url=http://bluemassgroup.com/showDiary.do?diaryId=4503 |title=Blue Mass. Group: Message to Kerry Healey: don't make him angry. You wouldn't like him when he's angry |access-date=2013-06-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011004800/http://bluemassgroup.com/showDiary.do?diaryId=4503 |archive-date=2007-10-11 |url-status=dead }} and documents leaked anonymously to media about Patrick's brother-in-law's criminal history. After the final debate, WRKO talk radio host John DePetro came under scrutiny for referring to Grace Ross as a "fat lesbian". DePetro had been suspended earlier in the year for calling Turnpike Authority chief Matt Amorello a "fag".[http://news.bostonherald.com/localRegional/view.bg?articleid=165497 'Fat lesbian' quip about Ross lands WRKO jock in hot water] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061108070454/http://news.bostonherald.com/localRegional/view.bg?articleid=165497 |date=November 8, 2006 }} ''Boston Herald'', November 3, 2006 ===Debates=== The first televised debate of the general election was held by [[WFXT]] and the ''[[Boston Herald]]'' on September 25 on [[WFXT]]. Moderated by Fox News' [[Chris Wallace (journalist)|Chris Wallace]] on the day after his [[Chris Wallace (journalist)#Bill Clinton interview|Bill Clinton interview]]. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Bob Ehrlich]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Martin O'Malley]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Maryland sidebar}} The '''2006 Maryland gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Bob Ehrlich]] ran for a second term, but was defeated by the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nominee, [[List of mayors of Baltimore|Baltimore Mayor]] [[Martin O'Malley]]. Ehrlich was the only incumbent governor to lose a general election in the 2006 midterms. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Martin O'Malley]], Mayor of [[Baltimore]] ===Campaign=== [[Baltimore]] Mayor [[Martin O'Malley]] and [[Montgomery County, Maryland|Montgomery County]] Executive [[Doug Duncan]] emerged as the two Democratic candidates for governor in late 2005. Early polling indicated that O'Malley would have the advantage in both the Democratic primary and the general election, with a solid lead over Duncan in the primary and a several point lead over Ehrlich in the general.{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2005/oct/24/20051024-103424-5071r/|title=Democrat support plunges for Ehrlich |newspaper=The Washington Times}} As the gubernatorial campaign intensified, Duncan withdrew from the race, citing his diagnosis with clinical depression. In the same announcement, he threw his support behind O'Malley and declined to seek another office in the fall. No other Democratic candidate had announced, so O'Malley was unopposed in the primary election. O'Malley selected [[Anthony Brown (Maryland politician)|Anthony Brown]], a black [[Maryland House of Delegates|State Delegate]] from [[Prince George's County, Maryland|Prince George's County]] and a veteran of the [[Iraq War]], as his running mate. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results{{Cite web|url=https://elections.maryland.gov/elections/2006/results/primary/office_Governor__Lt_Governor.html|title=Official 2006 Gubernatorial Primary Election results for Governor / Lt. Governor|website=elections.maryland.gov}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Martin O'Malley]] | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 524,671 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 524,671 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Bob Ehrlich]], incumbent [[Governor of Maryland|governor]] ===Campaign=== Ehrlich sought a second term as governor and did not face opposition at any point in the Republican primary. Incumbent [[Lieutenant Governor of Maryland|lieutenant governor]] [[Michael Steele]] [[2006 United States Senate election in Maryland|ran for the U.S. Senate]] instead of seeking a second term as lieutenant governor, so Ehrlich named Maryland Secretary of Disabilities [[Kristen Cox]], who is blind, as his running mate. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Bob Ehrlich]] (incumbent) | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 213,744 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 213,744 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box end}} ==General election== ===Candidates=== *[[Martin O'Malley]], Mayor of [[Baltimore]] (D) *[[Bob Ehrlich]], incumbent [[governor of Maryland]] (R) *Ed Boyd, temporary employment agency recruiter (G) *Christopher A. Driscoll (P) ===Campaign=== Elected to his first term in [[2002 Maryland gubernatorial election|2002]], incumbent Republican governor [[Bob Ehrlich]] ran for a second term as governor, opposed by the Democratic nominee, [[Martin O'Malley]], the mayor of [[Baltimore]]. Both candidates emerged from uncontested primary elections and a contentious election season began. Early in the campaign, Ehrlich boasted decent approval ratings from [[Maryland]] citizens, with a Gonzalez Research poll taken during October 2005 showing him with a 49% approval rating. and ''The Baltimore Sun'' poll from November 2005 giving the Governor a 50% approval and a 33% disapproval.{{Cite web|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2005/11/06/an-early-edge-for-ehrlichs-rivals/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250118182728/https://www.baltimoresun.com/2005/11/06/an-early-edge-for-ehrlichs-rivals/|url-status=live|archive-date=January 18, 2025|title=An early edge for Ehrlich's rivals|first=By Andrew A. Green and David|last=Nitkin|website=baltimoresun.com|url-access=subscription|date=November 6, 2005 }} However, the unpopularity of the national [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] and President [[George W. Bush]] dragged Ehrlich's re-election chances down.{{cite web |author1=Lauren Dezenski |author2=Kevin Robillard |title=Trump makes blue-state Republicans squirm |url=https://www.politico.com/story/2017/02/trump-hogan-baker-blue-states-234452 |website=[[Politico]] |access-date=16 July 2024 |date=1 February 2017}}{{cite news |author1=Matthew Mosk |author2=John Wagner |title=Cardin, O'Malley Win in Statewide Democratic Wave |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/2006/11/08/cardin-omalley-win-in-statewide-democratic-wave/745575ba-19e3-4434-8ead-cb2fa86a012d/ |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=16 July 2024 |date=8 November 2006 |quote=Although both contests remained competitive, the general anti-Republican mood pervading the nation began to weigh on Ehrlich and Steele, who tried to tap national GOP connections for money while trying to avoid an affiliation with Washington as the climate worsened for their party.}} Ehrlich launched attack ads that hit O'Malley on [[crime in Baltimore]] under his tenure as Mayor, calling the murder rate in Baltimore "awful" and "an embarrassment to the state of Maryland."{{Cite news|last=Wagner|first=John|date=2006-09-30|title=Ehrlich Ads Hammer O'Malley on Crime|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|language=en-US|url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/09/29/AR2006092901818.html|access-date=2021-07-16|issn=0190-8286}} O'Malley countered with one television ad that featured testimonials from local community leaders, [[Howard County, Maryland|Howard County]] Executive [[James N. Robey]], [[Baltimore County Executive]] [[James T. Smith Jr.]]{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1mb2FBF7Pwo |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211213/1mb2FBF7Pwo |archive-date=2021-12-13 |url-status=live|title=Martin O'Malley 2005 TV Ad: The Real Record in Baltimore|date=August 12, 2008 |via=www.youtube.com}}{{cbignore}} and another ad that attacked Ehrlich for breaking his promise to end parole for violent criminals.{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5DTH_Saas1I |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211213/5DTH_Saas1I |archive-date=2021-12-13 |url-status=live|title=Martin O'Malley 2005 TV Ad: The Real Question|date=August 12, 2008 |via=www.youtube.com}}{{cbignore}} ''[[The Washington Post]]'' and ''[[The Washington Times]]'' both endorsed Ehrlich in his bid for re-election, with the Times praising Ehrlich's "brand of moderate conservatism that offers a refreshing contrast" to the state's historically Democratic leanings{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2006/sep/6/20060906-100015-2449r/|title=Ehrlich for governor, Steele for Senate |newspaper=The Washington Times}} and the Post called him "a generally proficient, pragmatic governor" and praised him for "successes on transportation, the environment and education."{{Cite web|date=October 25, 2006|title=For Governor in Maryland|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/10/24/AR2006102401145.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070214204551/https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/10/24/AR2006102401145.html|archive-date=2007-02-14|access-date=|website=washingtonpost.com}} In turn, ''[[The Baltimore Sun]]'' endorsed O'Malley, saying, "the progress under the mayor's tenure is clear and irrefutable", and that he addressed "rising crime, failing schools and shrinking economic prospects."{{Cite web|date=October 29, 2006|title=O'Malley for governor|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2006/10/29/omalley-for-governor-2/|url-status=live|website=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|url-access=subscription|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201213624/http://articles.baltimoresun.com/2006-10-29/news/0610290023_1_omalley-rising-crime-slots-proposal |archive-date=2014-02-01 }} O'Malley also called upon the praise given to him by [[TIME Magazine]] when they named him one of the country's "Top 5 Big City Mayors."{{Cite [[Incumbent]] [[Maine Democratic Party|Democratic]] Governor [[John Baldacci]] won a second term, defeating [[Maine Republican Party|Republican]] nominee [[Chandler Woodcock]]. In the general election, Baldacci, Woodcock, Green Independent Party candidate [[Pat LaMarche]], and independents [[Barbara Merrill]] and Phillip Morris Napier appeared on the ballot. As of 2026, this is the last time [[Aroostook County, Maine|Aroostook]], [[Penobscot County, Maine|Penobscot]] and [[Oxford County, Maine|Oxford]] counties did not vote for the Republican gubernatorial nominee. This is also the last time until 2026 that [[Androscoggin County, Maine|Androscoggin County]] did not vote for the Republican gubernatorial nominee. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== * [[John [[Calais, Maine|Calais]]) ==Analysis== Despite the divided field, Baldacci still finished nearly eight points ahead of his nearest challenger, Woodcock. Merrill took an impressive 21% of the vote, and carried the municipalities of [[Glenwood Plantation, Maine|Glenwood Plantation]], [[Hope, Maine|Hope]], [[Milton, Maine|Milton]], [[Seboeis Plantation, Maine|Seboeis Plantation]], [[Stow, Maine|Stow]], [[The Forks, Maine|The Forks]], and [[Union, Maine|Union]]. Additionally, the municipalities of [[Carroll Plantation, Maine|Carroll Plantation]], [[Dennysville, Maine|Dennysville]], [[Wade, Maine|Wade]], and [[Westmanland, Maine|Westmanland]] finished as exact ties between Baldacci and Woodcock, while the municipality of [[Highland Plantation, Maine|Highland Plantation]] finished as an exact tie between Baldacci and LaMarche, the municipality of [[Webster Plantation, Maine|Webster Plantation]] finished as an exact tie between Baldacci and Merrill, and the municipality of [[Nashville Plantation, Maine|Nashville Plantation]] finished as an exact tie between Woodcock and Merrill. Despite LaMarche getting nearly 10% of the vote and slightly improving on [[Jonathan Carter (politician)|Jonathan Carter's]] vote percentage and vote total four years earlier, both of which were all-time highs for the [[Maine Green Independent Party]], the 2006 election remains the most recent time the Greens ran a candidate for governor. ==See also== * [[2006 United States gubernatorial elections]] * [[2006 United States Senate election in Maine]] ==Notes== {{notelist}} ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== '''Official campaign websites (archived)''' * [https://web.archive.org/web/20061004030617/http://baldacciforgovernor.com/ John Baldacci for Governor] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060823061058/http://www.woodcockforgovernor.com/ Chandler Woodcock for Governor] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060826120702/http://www.candidatebruce.com/ Bruce Fleming for Governor] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060824071717/http://www.hammer2006.politicalgateway.com/cand.php?id=426 Alex Hammer for Governor] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20061004034045/http://barbaramerrill.com/ Barbara Merrill for Governor] * [https://web.archive.org/web/20060905060010/http://www.jonesforgovernor.org/ David Jones for Governor] {{Maine gubernatorial elections|state=expanded}} {{2006 U.S. midterm elections}} {{US Third Party Election}} [[Category:2006 elections in Maine|Governor]] [[Category:Maine gubernatorial elections|2006]] [[Category:2006 United States gubernatorial elections|Maine]]
