Cherry]], incumbent lieutenant governor === Campaign === [[File:Betsy Devos.jpg|thumb|Dick DeVos' wife, [[Betsy DeVos|Betsy]], with a supporter at a campaign event in [[Houghton County, Michigan|Houghton County]]]] After her first election as governor in [[2002 Michigan gubernatorial election|2002]], Granholm was widely seen as a rising star in the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]]. Her popularity dropped after she took office in 2003, largely due to a weak economy and high unemployment. In August 2006, her approval rating was 47 percent.{{cite web | url=http://strategicvision.biz/political/michigan_poll_082906.htm | title=Strategic Vision Political | access-date=2006-11-09 | date=August 27, 2006 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902045345/http://www.strategicvision.biz/political/michigan_poll_082906.htm | archive-date=September 2, 2006 }} DeVos, a multimillionaire, had developed substantial political contacts with the full participation of his wife, former [[Michigan Republican Party]] chair [[Betsy DeVos]], despite which, fully 85% of the DeVos campaign's contributions were from DeVos' inheritance.Land, Terri Lynn (Michigan Secretary of State). [http://miboecfr.nictusa.com/cgi-bin/cfr/com_det.cgi?com_id=512426 " Campaign Finance Disclosure"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081108073844/http://miboecfr.nictusa.com/cgi-bin/cfr/com_det.cgi?com_id=512426 |date=2008-11-08 }} As the 2006 election approached, the DeVos family was listed among the biggest Republican campaign contributors in Michigan.{{cite web|title=DeVoses pour millions into GOP causes |date=June 18, 2006 |access-date=2006-11-09 |work=Detroit Free Press |url=http://www.freep.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20060618/NEWS06/606180604/1008 |author=Christoff, Chris |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060627023047/http://www.freep.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20060618%2FNEWS06%2F606180604%2F1008 |archive-date=June 27, 2006 }} The DeVos campaign spent $42.5 million, at that time the most spent on a gubernatorial campaign in Michigan history. $35.5 million of that total came from DeVos' personal fortune, and was at that time the most spent personally by a Republican candidate running for governor. The Granholm campaign spent $15.7 million. The combined money spent by both campaigns made this the most expensive gubernatorial election in Michigan history. As DeVos funded his campaign himself, he was not eligible for public funds.{{cite web | url=http://www.mcfn.org/pdfs/reports/07_MCFN_Cit_Guide.pdf | title=2006 Citizen's Guide to Michigan Campaign Finance | work=Michigan Campaign Finance Network | date=18 July 2007 | access-date=18 January 2015 | archive-date=5 December 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205140450/http://www.mcfn.org/pdfs/reports/07_MCFN_Cit_Guide.pdf | url-status=live }} The DeVos and Campbell campaigns each made the state's economy their major issue. DeVos criticized the Single Business Tax, high unemployment, and job outsourcing which occurred during Granholm's first term; Campbell assailed the $12 billion taken from Michigan's taxpayers and appropriated to the military siege of Iraq (which he calls "Duh-bya's Folly") and advocated for a local currency, independent of the U.S. dollar which he and running mate David Skrbina say is in imminent jeopardy of collapse. Granholm countered that her policies saved thousands of jobs. She also attacked DeVos's partisanship, wealth, and tenure at Alticor. One of Granholm's most prominent lines of attack was the accusation that Alticor, under DeVos's tenure, outsourced thousands of jobs to China while cutting 1,400 jobs in Michigan, a charge that the DeVos campaign and numerous media factcheckers denied. DeVos, Campbell and Granholm criticized the [[Michigan Civil Rights Initiative]] which was exclusively supported by Creswell,Creswell, Gregory [http://gregcreswell.lpwm.org/racial-preferences "Equal Means Equal"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061206201628/http://gregcreswell.lpwm.org/racial-preferences |date=2006-12-06 }}. ''lpwm.org'' (website).Creswell, Gregory [http://gregcreswell.org "campaign site"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061213193453/http://www.gregcreswell.org/ |date=2006-12-13 }}. "gregcreswell.org" (website). and passed by a wide margin.Land, Terri (Secretary of State).[http://miboecfr.nictusa.com/election/results/06GEN/90000002.html "State Proposal – 06-2: Constitutional Amendment: Ban Affirmative Action Programs"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090410025447/http://miboecfr.nictusa.com/election/results/06GEN/90000002.html |date=2009-04-10 }}. ''mi.gov'' (website). On August 25, 2006, [[Detroit]] Mayor [[Kwame Kilpatrick]] pledged to actively campaign for Granholm and utilize the campaign team which got him re-elected as mayor.[http://detnews.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20060825/POLITICS01/608250340 Detnews.com | This article is no longer available online] The Michigan Democratic Party held their state convention in city of [[Detroit]] at [[Cobo Hall]], while the Michigan Republican Party held their convention in the City of [[Novi, Michigan|Novi]] in [[Oakland County]] at the new Rock Financial Showplace. In October 2006, the Creswell campaign spent over $10,000 on radio advertising, which while small, was the most spent on a such advertising by any Michigan gubernatorial campaign outside the Democratic or Republican parties.http://miboecfr.nicusa.com/cfr/dumpimages/2784121.pdf {{dead link|date=August 2012}}Land, Terri (Secretary of State).[http://miboecfr.nicusa.com/cgi-bin/cfr/gub_search.cgi "Gubernatorial Committee Search"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061209100027/http://miboecfr.nicusa.com/cgi-bin/cfr/gub_search.cgi |date=2006-12-09 }}. "mi.gov" (website) The largest investment was made in advertisements on [[Detroit]] AM Radio stations [[WJR]] and [[WXYT (AM)|WXYT]].http://miboecfr.nicusa.com/cfr/dumpimages/2805101.pdf {{dead link|date=August 2012}} These commercials specifically targeted Devos and Granholm by referring to them as candidates of "The two old parties," and berating them for supporting state-supported preferences based on race and sex: A clear reference to [[Michigan Civil Rights Initiative|MCRI]].Creswell, Gregory [http://gregcreswell.lpwm.org/copy_of_Audio/copy_of_radio_ad.mp3/view "Radio Commercial In Use"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061207024340/http://gregcreswell.lpwm.org/copy_of_Audio/copy_of_radio_ad.mp3/view |date=2006-12-07 }}. "gregcreswell.lpwm.org" (website) Campbell spent less than $1,000,http://miboecfr.nicusa.com/cfr/dumpimages/2743511.pdf {{dead link|date=August 2012}} as was the case with the Dashairya campaign.http://miboecfr.nicusa.com/cfr/dumpimages/2802601.pdf {{dead link|date=August 2012}} ===Debates=== [[File:GranDebate.jpg|thumb|left|alt=Granholm and Devos at an October 12 informal debate at the Detroit Economic Club|Granholm and Devos at an October 12 informal debate at the Detroit Economic Club]] The DeVos and Granholm campaigns agreed to three televised debates and a single joint appearance. This agreement did not include any provision for participation by third-party candidates.{{cite web | title=Agreement Governing Debates and Joint Appearances in Michigan's 2006 Gubernatorial Campaign | url=http://woodtv.triton.net/news/debate/agreement.pdf | work=[[WOOD-TV]] | access-date=January 18, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303170602/http://woodtv.triton.net/news/debate/agreement.pdf | archive-date=2016-03-03 }} Granholm and DeVos appeared together October 12 at the [[Detroit Economic Club]] in which each candidate delivered their job plans, which was described as a debate at the event itself, even if it wasn't officially designated as such.{{cite news | url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1350&dat=20061013&id=tnhhAAAAIBAJ&pg=6708,3362642 | title=Granholm, DeVos find common ground on 1 topic | work=[[Toledo Blade]] | date=October 13, 2006 | access-date=18 January 2015 | archive-date=6 October 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221006122433/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1350&dat=20061013&id=tnhhAAAAIBAJ&pg=6708,3362642 | url-status=live }} ====WKAR-TV debate==== The first debate occurred on October 2 at [[WKAR-TV]] in [[East Lansing, Michigan|East Lansing]].{{cite news | title=A Special Broadcast from WKAR | url=http://www.wkar.org/specials/debateforgovernor/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061006124328/http://wkar.org/specials/debateforgovernor/ | archive-date=October 6, 2006 | work=[[WKAR-TV]]}} Both candidates spent the hour trading charges and countercharges. ''[[Detroit News]]'' pollster Ed Sarpolus indicated that there was no clear winner in the debate, but Bill Rustem, senior vice president of the nonpartisan policy firm Public Sector Consultants in Lansing, favored Granholm.http://www.detnews.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20061003/POLITICS01/610030400 {{Dead link|date=July 2022}} The consensus of pundits Bill Ballenger, George Bullard, Kathy Barks Hoffman and Rick Albin and capital correspondent Tim Skubick, speaking on the October 6 WKAR-television program Off the Record,{{cite web |url=http://wkar.org/offtherecord/program.php?num=2007-14 |title = Off the Record |access-date=2007-09-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061006134359/https://wkar.org/offtherecord/program.php?num=2007-14 |archive-date=2006-10-06 }} was that both DeVos and Granholm emerged losers, losing 2 and 4 percentage points' support after the event. No major gaffes or zingers came out in the debate. Some of the positions were made clear on embryonic stem cell research {{cite web |url=http://www.lsj.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20061003/NEWS01/610030335/1312 |title= Lansing State Journal - Home|website=www.lsj.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061004003635/http://www.lsj.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20061003%2FNEWS01%2F610030335%2F1312 |archive-date=2006-10-04}} and abortion.{{cite web |url=http://www.theoaklandpress.com/stories/100306/loc_2006100327.shtml |title = The Oakland Press: Local News |access-date=2006-10-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061021174925/http://www.theoaklandpress.com/stories/100306/loc_2006100327.shtml |archive-date=2006-10-21 }} No major gaffes came out in the debate, but one minor zinger was made by Granholm about DeVos' investment in Alterra, a chain of nursing homes which sexually abused and neglected its patients.http://www.detnews.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20061004/POLITICS01/610040369 {{Dead link|date=July 2022}}{{cite news |url=http://www.mlive.com/news/grpress/index.ssf?%2Fbase%2Fnews-32%2F1160206504163180.xml&coll=6 |title= |newspaper=Grand Rapids Press |access-date=2006-10-08 |archive-date=2016-03-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304050253/http://www.mlive.com/news/grpress/index.ssf?%2Fbase%2Fnews-32%2F1160206504163180.xml&coll=6 |url-status=dead }} ====WOOD-TV debate==== The second was October 10 at [[WOOD-TV]] in [[Grand Rapids, Michigan|Grand Rapids]]. DeVos was more aggressive than before, declaring that Granholm had lied about him having a controlling stake in Alterra Health Care, an elder-care company that suppressed information about the abuse of residents by its employees.{{cite web |url=http://www.mlive.com/news/grpress/index.ssf?/base/news-32/116057011613340.xml&coll=6&thispage=2 |title=Archived copy |website=www.mlive.com |access-date=22 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930153914/http://www.mlive.com/news/grpress/index.ssf?/base/news-32/116057011613340.xml&coll=6&thispage=2 |archive-date=30 September 2007 }} According to SEC filings, DeVos and his investment partners jointly owned 40% of Alterra stock totalling $173 million.{{cite web |url=http://sec.edgar-online.com/2001/04/30/0000950144-01-501321/Section9.asp |title = ALTERRA HEALTHCARE CORP Amended Annual Report (10-K/A) ITEM 12 SECURITY OWNERSHIP OF CERTAIN BENEFICIAL OWNERS AND ... |access-date=2006-10-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071001005040/http://sec.edgar-online.com/2001/04/30/0000950144-01-501321/Section9.asp |archive-date=2007-10-01 }} The chairman of Alterra's board, while a close associate of DeVos, nevertheless maintains that DeVos had no part of running the company himself.{{cite news |url=http://www.mlive.com/news/muchronicle/index.ssf?%2Fbase%2Fnews-5%2F1160059527159120.xml&coll=8&thispage=1 |title= |newspaper=Muskegon Chronicle |access-date=2006-10-12 |archive-date=2007-09-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930155014/http://www.mlive.com/news/muchronicle/index.ssf?%2Fbase%2Fnews-5%2F1160059527159120.xml&coll=8&thispage=1 |url-status=dead }} DeVos also asserted that he had convinced President Bush to set a date to meet with the three major Michigan auto companies. Granholm responded that she did not believe that was true. DeVos admitted after the debate that he misspoke; the president agreed to have a meeting at some point after the election, but did not confirm a date.{{cite web |url=http://www.ludingtondailynews.com/news.php?story_id=33320 |title=Ludington Daily News {{!}} shorelinemedia.net |access-date=2006-10-11 |archive-date=2012-02-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120205185025/http://www.ludingtondailynews.com/news.php?story_id=33320 |url-status=live }} On October 24, two weeks after this debate was held, a mid-November date was set for the meeting.http://www.detnews.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20061025/AUTO01/610250385 {{Dead link|date=July 2022}} ====WXYZ-TV debate==== The third televised debate was October 16 at [[WXYZ-TV]] in [[Southfield, Michigan|Southfield]]. Unlike the previous debates, this one had an invited studio audience of 30 undecided voters, some of whom asked questions to the participating candidates. Like the two previous debates, only two of the five candidates were admitted.{{cite news|first=Mike |last=Ellis |title=Tonight's debate will lack three candidates: Campbell, Dashairya, Creswell also weren't invited to first two |date=October 16, 2006 |publisher=Central Michigan University |url=http://www.cm-life.com/home/index.cfm?event=displayArticle&ustory_id=c97c23df-80bd-44d2-8560-8bca8249e39e |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927005034/http://www.cm-life.com/home/index.cfm?event=displayArticle&ustory_id=c97c23df-80bd-44d2-8560-8bca8249e39e |archive-date=2007-09-27 }}{{Cite web |url=http://www.detnow.com/wxyz/nw_local_news/article/0,2132,WXYZ_15924_5070251,00.html |title = WXYZ: Local News |access-date=2006-10-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061023003027/http://www.detnow.com/wxyz/nw_local_news/article/0,2132,WXYZ_15924_5070251,00.html |archive-date=2006-10-23 }} Granholm and DeVos sparred on various issues including college tuition, Canadian trash, business taxes, [[George W. Bush|President Bush]] and negative ads,{{cite web |url=http://freep.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20061016/NEWS99/61016049 |title= Error: Invalid story key (C4,20061016,NEWS99,61016049,AR)|website=freep.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929122248/http://freep.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20061016%2FNEWS99%2F61016049 |archive-date=2007-09-29}} while Creswell supporters picketed outside.{{cite news | first=Scotty | last=Boman | title=Mobalize On October 16th. Make WXYZ take notice | date=October 3, 2006 | publisher=Libertarian Party of Michigan | url=http://mi.lp.org/ENewsletters/N20061003.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080918045917/http://www.mi.lp.org/ENewsletters/N20061003.htm | archive-date=September 18, 2008 | df=mdy-all }}{{Cite web |url=http://michiganlp.org/Pictures/_w/October_16_debate_JPG.jpg |title=Archived copy |access-date=2007-07-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928094604/http://michiganlp.org/Pictures/_w/October_16_debate_JPG.jpg |archive-date=2007-09-28 }}{{Cite web |url=http://michiganlp.org/Pictures/_w/debate_night_jpg.jpg |title=Archived copy |access-date=2007-07-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928094556/http://michiganlp.org/Pictures/_w/debate_night_jpg.jpg |archive-date=2007-09-28 }}{{cite web |url=http://gregcreswell.lpwm.org/greg-campaigning/copy_of_wxyz/view |title = wxyz — Campaign Template |access-date=2007-07-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928014548/http://gregcreswell.lpwm.org/greg-campaigning/copy_of_wxyz/view |archive-date=2007-09-28 }} During the opening statements of the third debate, Gov. Granholm attacked DeVos for using pictures of dead children as a campaign tool against her. However, it was later revealed that DeVos was not the person using the pictures, but supporters of him, who were cheering for him outside of the debate studio. ====CMN-TV (of Troy) debate==== On October 18 CMN-TV in [[Troy, Michigan|Troy]] broadcast an additional debate.{{citation needed|date=January 2015}} This debate was not covered by the agreement between the DeVos and Granholm campaigns. It was the only televised debate to which all gubernatorial candidates were invited. It also was only the only televised debate in which the majority of gubernatorial candidates participated. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Tim Pawlenty]] | before_party = Republican Party of Minnesota | after_election = [[Tim Pawlenty]] | after_party = Republican Party of Minnesota }} {{ElectionsMN}} The '''2006 Minnesota gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006 to elect the governor and lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Republican incumbent [[Tim Pawlenty]] was re-elected to a second term over Mike Hatch. This was the closest race of the [[2006 United States gubernatorial elections|2006 gubernatorial election cycle]]. {{As of|2026}}, this is the last time a Republican won a statewide race in Minnesota. ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== * [[Sue Jeffers]], [[Minneapolis]] bar owner ** Running mate: Ruth Hendrycks * [[Tim Pawlenty]], incumbent [[governor of Minnesota]] since 2003 ** Running mate: [[Carol Molnau]], incumbent l[[Lieutenant Governor of Minnesota|lieutenant governor of Minnesota]] since 2003 === Campaign === Pawlenty was challenged by [[Sue Jeffers]], a libertarian activist noted for her opposition for smoking bans and the use of eminent domain. Although Jeffers was cross-endorsed by the Libertarian Party and the Republican Liberty Caucus, Minnesota law does not allow fusion candidates. She did not participate in the party endorsement process but chose to run directly against Pawlenty in the September primary. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change |title = Republican gubernatorial primary election, 2006 }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Tim Pawlenty (incumbent) | party = Republican Party of Minnesota | votes = 147,622 | percentage = 88.87 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Sue Jeffers | party = Republican Party of Minnesota | votes = 18,490 | percentage = 11.13 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 166,112 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==DFL primary== ===Candidates=== * [[Mike Hatch]], [[Minnesota Attorney General|Minnesota attorney general]] since 1999 ** Running mate: [[Judi Dutcher]], [[Minnesota State Auditor|Minnesota state auditor]] since 1995 * [[Becky Lourey]], [[Minnesota Senate|state senator]] ** Running mate: [[Tim Baylor]], businessman and former [[Minnesota Vikings]] [[defensive back]] * Ole Savior, artist and [[perennial candidate]] ** Running mate: Dan Fischer ====Withdrawn==== * [[Kelly Doran]], [[real estate developer]] (''withdrew March 24, 2006'') * [[Steve Kelley (politician)|Steve Kelley]], [[Minnesota Senate|state senator]] (''withdrew June 10 following loss at convention; endorsed Hatch'') * Bud Philbrook, former [[Minnesota House of Representatives|state representative]] (1975–77) (''withdrew October 24, 2005'') === Campaign === Hatch received the strongest support of all candidates in the statewide precinct caucus straw poll and continued to hold his lead into the party convention, at which he received the endorsement after seven ballots. Lourey continued to seek the DFL nomination in the primary election. Ole Savior was eliminated on the first ballot after winning just one vote out of 1,500, but he continued to seek the nomination in the primary. Steve Kelley withdrew his candidacy on June 10, and endorsed Hatch. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change |title = Democratic–Farmer–Labor gubernatorial primary election, 2006{{cite Soderberg * [[Mike Hatch]], [[Minnesota Attorney General|Minnesota attorney general]] since 1999 (DFL) ** Running mate: [[Judi Dutcher]], [[Minnesota State Auditor|Minnesota state auditor]] since 1995 * [[Peter Hutchinson (politician)|Peter Hutchinson]], former [[Minnesota Department of Revenue|Minnesota commissioner of finance]] and superintendent of [[Minneapolis Public Schools]] (Independence) ** Running mate: [[Maureen Reed]], former chair of the [[University of Minnesota]] [[Board of Regents]] * [[Tim Pawlenty]], incumbent [[governor of Minnesota]] since 2003 (Republican) ** Running mate: [[Carol Molnau]], incumbent l[[Lieutenant Governor of Minnesota|lieutenant governor of Minnesota]] since 2003 * Ken Pentel ([[Green Party of Minnesota|Green]]) ** Running mate: Danene Provencher ==== Withdrew ==== * [[Jonathon Sharkey]], self-proclaimed [[vampire]] and perennial candidate Sharkey's campaign was jeopardized on January 30, when he was arrested in [[Princeton, Minnesota]] on felony charges stemming from allegations in Indiana of [[stalking]] and flight.{{cite web |url=http://wcco.com/topstories/local_story_031105113.html |title = wcco.com - 'Impaler' Claims He Did Nothing Wrong |access-date=June 18, 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060716080857/http://wcco.com/topstories/local_story_031105113.html |archive-date=July 16, 2006 }} His campaign website was taken down, and it was discovered that the stalking charge had been dismissed on September 29, 2003, when Sharkey pleaded guilty to two counts of invasion of privacy and was ordered to submit to mental health treatment.[http://www.theimpalerforpresident2008.us/images/Dismissal_of_Charges.JPG Scanned copy of Prosecutor's Motion to Dismiss] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090324192213/http://www.theimpalerforpresident2008.us/images/Dismissal_of_Charges.JPG |date=March 24, 2009 }}{{cite web|url=http://www.in.gov/judiciary/opinions/pdf/12110605jts.pdf|title=Sharkey v. Indiana, Ind. App. (2006)|website=in.gov|access-date=April 6, 2018}} On July 18, 2006, he was found not guilty of the felony escape charge. His arrest and jailing effectively terminated his campaign. === Campaign === After Pawlenty opted out of spending limits, Hatch followed suit. Outspending Hatch by $1 million, Pawlenty's campaign set a new spending record for a Minnesota gubernatorial campaign. The race was also affected by negative advertising by 527 groups, as well as issue-oriented groups opposing liberal causes in the state. A major issue in the campaign that was considered to have hurt the DFL nominees was lieutenant gubernatorial candidate [[Judi Dutcher]]'s response to a question about [[E-85]]. When asked about the impact of the gasoline alternative on the economies of rural Minnesota by then [[KSAX-TV]] anchor [[Corey Poppe]], Dutcher was unable to comment, asking Poppe to define E-85.{{cite web|url=http://www.startribune.com/587/story/784334.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061114135949/http://www.startribune.com/587/story/784334.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 14, 2006|title=GOP jumps on Dutcher's E85 misstep|date=November 14, 2006|access-date=April 6, 2018}} In the subsequent questioning about her response, gubernatorial candidate [[Mike Hatch]] reportedly called a Forum Communications reporter "a Republican whore" and promptly hung up the phone.http://www.duluthnewstribune.com/articles/index.cfm?id=27509&freebie_check&CFID=4612252&CFTOKEN=43846502&jsessionid=8830d400afe52687c441{{dead link|date=February 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}http://www.startribune.com/blogs/kersten/?p=37{{dead link|date=February 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Hatch claimed he had said "hack", not "whore", but the incident, occurring only three days before the last poll listed in this article, is believed to have swung the race. It put Hatch on the defensive in the campaign's last week. Additionally, Pawlenty made illegal immigration an issue, running ads accusing Hatch of trying to give illegal immigrants college tuition. Hatch responded with an ad saying that illegal immigration laws had not been enforced under Pawlenty's tenure. Pawlenty also ran ads accusing Hatch of being responsible for raising [[health care prices in the United States|health care costs]], a claim Hatch disputed. Pawlenty campaigned on a record of leading the state through hard times, balancing record budget deficits without raising major state tax rates or diminishing the state's "nation-leading" status on most socioeconomic indicators. === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- ! Hutchinson won 6.4 percent of the vote. Pawlenty won by piling up large margins in suburban counties as well as in central and southern Minnesota regions anchored by [[St. Cloud, Minnesota|St. Cloud]] and [[Rochester, Minnesota|Rochester]]. In his victory speech, noting that he would have to deal with a DFL [[85th Minnesota Legislature|House and Senate]], Pawlenty said it was "a time tonight to be humble and time to be grateful." He promised that "the next four years are going to be different than the last four years" and that he would build "a common agenda" with the DFL candidates who swept legislative and constitutional offices. Hatch ran ahead in [[Minneapolis]], [[Saint Paul, Minnesota|St. Paul]] and their inner-ring suburbs, and won by large margins around [[Duluth, Minnesota|Duluth]] and the [[Iron Range]]. In his concession speech, Hatch advocated that legislators get back to "sitting down and getting to know each other in private" to establish common ground for bipartisan legislation and called for an end to partisan rancor.{{cite web |url=http://www.startribune.com/10134/story/786531.html |title = Hatch concedes to Pawlenty |access-date=November 8, 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070926222607/http://www.startribune.com/10134/story/786531.html |archive-date=September 26, 2007 }}[[file:Minnesota gubernatorial election, 2006 Independence Party.svg|thumb|right|280px|County results for the Independence Party: {{collapsible list | title = Hutchinson |{{legend0|#ffb580|<4%%}} |{{legend0|#ff9a50|4-5%}} |{{legend0|#ff8450|5-6%}} |{{legend0|#ff7350|6-7%}} |{{legend0|#d76143|7-8%}} |{{legend0|#ae4e36|8%<}} }}]] {{Election box begin no change | title= Minnesota gubernatorial election, 2006{{cite web|url=http://electionresults.sos.state.mn.us/Results/Governor/55?officeInElectionId=1706|title=MN Election Results|website=electionresults.sos.state.mn.us|access-date=April 6, 2018}}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change |party = Republican Party of Minnesota |candidate = [[Tim Pawlenty]] (incumbent) |votes = 1,028,568 |percentage = 46.69 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change |party = Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party |candidate = [[Mike Hatch]] |votes = 1,007,460 |percentage = 45.73 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change |party = Independence Party of Minnesota |candidate = [[Peter Hutchinson (politician)|Peter Hutchinson]] |votes = 141,735 |percentage = 6.43 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change |party = Green Party of Minnesota |candidate = Ken Pentel |votes = 10,800 |percentage = 0.49 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change |party = Independent |candidate = Walt E. '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} }} {{ElectionsNE}} The '''2006 Nebraska gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006; the [[Partisan primary|primary election]] was held on May 9, 2006. Republican incumbent [[Dave Heineman]] was re-elected to a full term, defeating Democrat [[David Hahn (American politician)|David Hahn]]. ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Dave Heineman]], incumbent [[Governor of Nebraska]] *Dave Nabity, financial consultant, former Young Republicans state chair *[[Tom Osborne]], U.S. Congressman, former football coach ===Campaign=== The Republican primary election had the unusual situation of an incumbent running against several members of his own party. Originally, the 2006 election would not have had an incumbent. However, this changed when [[Mike Johanns]] resigned in January 2005 to become [[United States Secretary of Agriculture]]; this elevated [[Lieutenant Governor of Nebraska|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Dave Heineman]] to the governorship. He then announced his intention to run for election to a full four-year term. The other two candidates for the Republican nomination were former [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football]] coach [[Tom Osborne]]—then serving in the [[United States House of Representatives]]—and Omaha businessman Dave Nabity. In 2005, the three Republican candidates raised more than $2 million overall for their campaigns: Osborne $972,000; Heineman $922,000; and Nabity $150,000. Osborne named [[Kate Witek]], the [[Nebraska State Auditor]], as his running mate for the office of lieutenant governor.{{citation|author=Don Walton|title=Witek leaves GOP to join Dems|newspaper=Lincoln Journal Star|date=August 18, 2006|page=15|access-date=June 22, 2023|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/298172594/}} She had previously been the running mate of Gene Spence in the [[1994 Nebraska gubernatorial election]]. After the Osborne-Witek ticket was unsuccessful in the Republican primaries, Witek switched parties and joined the Democratic party. ===Results=== [[File:2006 Nebraska Gubernatorial election Republican primary results map by county.svg|thumb|300px|center|Primary results by county. {{collapsible list |title=Map legend |{{legend|#D72F30|Heineman—70–80%}} |{{legend|#D75D5D|Heineman—60–70%}} |{{legend|#E27F7F|Heineman—50–60%}} |{{legend|#FFB2B2|Heineman—40–50%}} |{{legend|#FFB580|Osborne—40–50%}} |{{legend|#FF9A50|Osborne—50–60%}} }} ]] {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican Party primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Dave Heineman]] (incumbent) | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 138,216 | percentage = 50.26 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Tom Osborne]] | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 121,973 | percentage = 44.36 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Dave Nabity | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 14,786 | percentage = 5.38 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 274,975 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *Glenn R. Boot Jr., truck driver *[[David Hahn (American politician)|David Hahn]], attorney and internet development company CEO ===Campaign=== The Democratic primary election did not have any candidates until December 2005, when [[David Hahn (Nebraska)|David Hahn]] announced his candidacy. Glenn Boot Jr. of [[Ashland, Nebraska|Ashland]] was the other Democratic candidate, but he was disqualified due to a previous felony conviction. The election was not a high priority for Nebraska Democrats. While the main reason was focusing on getting [[United States Senate|U.S. Senator]] [[Ben Nelson]] reelected, it was very likely that most Democrats didn't want to face the possibility of running against the immensely popular Osborne. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic Party primary results{{cite web |url=http://www.sos.ne.gov/elec/canvass/primary2006/GOV.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071114204943/http://www.sos.ne.gov/elec/canvass/primary2006/GOV.htm |archive-date=2007-11-14 |title=Governor}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = David Hahn | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 68,004 | percentage = 91.57 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Glenn R. '''Dendahl''': {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} | title = [[List of governors of New Mexico|Governor]] | before_election = [[Bill Richardson]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Bill Richardson]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsNM}} The '''2006 New Mexico gubernatorial election''' was a race for the [[governor of New Mexico]] held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Bill Richardson]] was running for re-election. He faced Republican [[John Dendahl]] in the general election and won by a landslide. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this was the last time a male candidate was elected Governor of New Mexico. The scale of Richardson's lopsided victory was nearly unprecedented in the traditionally competitive state. Richardson's 68.82% share of the vote is the highest achieved by any gubernatorial candidate in the state by a wide margin, beating the previous record of 60.21% set in [[1964 New Mexico gubernatorial election|1964]]. Richardson came within six votes of sweeping every county in the state, a feat that has never been achieved in any gubernatorial (or presidential) election in the state. ==Primary election== ===Democratic party=== ====Candidates==== *[[Bill Richardson (politician)|Bill Richardson]], incumbent [[governor of New Mexico]] *Anselmo A. Incumbent [[Governor of Nevada|Governor]] [[Kenny Guinn]] could not run due to [[Term limits in the United States|term limits]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] Congressman [[Jim Gibbons (American politician)|Jim Gibbons]] defeated [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] State Senator [[Dina Titus]]. '''Faso''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[George Pataki]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Eliot Spitzer]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in New York (state) sidebar}} The '''2006 New York gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006, to elect the governor and lieutenant governor of New York. Then-incumbent Republican governor [[George Pataki]] chose not to run for re-election in a fourth term. Democrat [[Eliot Spitzer]], the [[Attorney General of New York|New York Attorney General]], won the election over former Republican state Assembly minority leader [[John Faso]]. Primary elections were held on September 12. This was the first open-seat election since [[1982 New York gubernatorial election|1982]]. This is the last gubernatorial election where any of the following counties voted Democratic: [[Genesee County, New York|Genesee]], [[Chautauqua County, New York|Chautauqua]], [[Cattaraugus County, New York|Cattaraugus]], [[Niagara County, New York|Niagara]], [[Fulton County, New York|Fulton]], [[Steuben County, New York|Steuben]], [[Tioga County, New York|Tioga]], and [[Schoharie County, New York|Schoharie]]. Spitzer was slated to serve between January 1, 2007, and December 31, 2010, but he announced his resignation on March 12, 2008 (effective March 17, 2008), amid news of his involvement in a [[Eliot Spitzer prostitution scandal|prostitution scandal]]. Spitzer was succeeded on March 17 by [[Lieutenant Governor of New York|Lieutenant Governor]] [[David Paterson]]. == Republican primary == === Candidates === *[[John Faso]], former New York Assembly minority leader (1998–2002) and Republican nominee for [[New York State Comptroller|Comptroller]] in 2002 **Running mate: C. Scott Vanderhoef, Rockland County Executive ==== Withdrew ==== *[[Randy Daniels]], Secretary of the State of New York *[[Patrick R. Manning]], Assemblyman from [[Dutchess County, New York|Dutchess County]] *[[Bill Weld]], former Governor of Massachusetts (following loss at convention) ==== Declined ==== * [[Tom Golisano]], businessman and Independence Party nominee for Governor in 1994, 1998, and 2002 * [[George Pataki]], incumbent Governor since 1995 (declined on July 27, 2005) * [[Donald Trump]], president of the [[The Trump Organization|Trump Organization]] and host of ''[[The Apprentice (American TV series)|The Apprentice]]'' (Democratic Party; endorsed Eliot Spitzer) === Campaign === Following the early campaign announcement of Attorney General Eliot Spitzer in late 2004, attention turned to the state Republican Party, especially the future of three-term governor [[George Pataki]]. Polling throughout 2004 and into 2005 consistently showed Spitzer defeating Pataki in theoretical matchups. Pataki announced on July 27, 2005, that he would not seek re-election and would step down at the end of his term in January 2007. In 2005, John Faso announced his intention to run for governor. He positioned himself early as a conservative upstate candidate, while stressing his childhood roots in [[Long Island]]. He initially faced former Massachusetts Governor [[Bill Weld]], former Secretary of State [[Randy Daniels]], and Assemblyman Patrick Manning. Weld, a moderate, was supported by party leadership.{{Cite news |last=Healy |first=Patrick |date=June 2, 2006 |title=State G.O.P. Convention Rebuffs Weld and Backs Faso for Governor |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/06/02/nyregion/02gov.html |via=NYTimes.com}} On February 14, Faso launched a statewide campaign ad announcing his candidacy for governor. Later that month, he was endorsed by Conservative Party Chairman Michael Long and by Congressman [[John E. Sweeney|John Sweeney]].{{Cite news |last=Hakim |first=Danny |date=February 22, 2006 |title=Weld Suffers Two Setbacks to Candidacy in One Day |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/02/22/nyregion/weld-suffers-two-setbacks-to-candidacy-in-one-day.html |via=NYTimes.com}} Daniels and Manning both dropped out and Faso became the primary challenger to Weld. It was reported that in early 2006, Weld offered Faso the chance to join his ticket as a candidate for [[Lieutenant Governor of New York|lieutenant governor]], an offer Faso reportedly declined.{{Cite web |date=December 13, 2006 |title=New York State Democratic Committee |url=http://www.nydems.org/news/archive/2006_06_001431.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061213233211/http://www.nydems.org/news/archive/2006_06_001431.html |archive-date=2006-12-13}} Faso gained increasing support from party leaders in various counties, including [[Westchester County, New York|Westchester]] and [[Suffolk County, New York|Suffolk]], both of which had large delegate counts to the state convention. In late May 2006, Faso received the nomination of the Conservative Party for governor, which guaranteed him a spot on the November ballot. He pledged to continue running for governor on the Conservative line if he lost the Republican primary to Weld.{{Cite news |last=Healy |first=Patrick D. |date=February 9, 2006 |title=In Weld's Bid, G.O.P. Risks Losing Conservative Party Allies |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/02/09/nyregion/in-welds-bid-gop-risks-losing-conservative-party-allies.html |via=NYTimes.com}} On the day he received the Conservative nomination, Faso announced his selection of Rockland County Executive C. Scott Vanderhoef as his [[running mate]] for lieutenant governor. On June 1, 2006, the Republican State Convention voted 61% to 39% to endorse Faso. By receiving over 50 percent of the vote, Faso was the designated Republican Party candidate, but Weld still received enough support to force a primary. As ''[[The Washington Post]]'' put it, "[n]ow it turns out whoever loses the GOP primary will stay in the race—in a position likely to siphon votes from the Republican nominee."{{cite news |title=Another Stumble for Ralph Reed's Beleaguered Campaign |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/05/28/AR2006052800964.html}} For this reason, Weld was under tremendous pressure to drop out of the race. On June 5, [[Stephen J. Minarik]], the chairman of the state Republican Party, who had been Weld's most prominent backer, called on Weld to withdraw in the interest of party unity.{{cite news |last=Healy |first=Patrick |date=June 5, 2006 |title=G.O.P. Chief in N.Y. Urges Weld to Quit Governor's Race |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/06/05/nyregion/05cnd-gov.html |access-date=August 5, 2008}} Weld formally announced his withdrawal from the race, and his support of Faso, the following day.{{cite web |date=2006-06-06 |title=Former Mass. Gov. Weld drops out of New York race |url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/06/06/AR2006060600786.html |access-date=2021-04-06 |website=washingtonpost.com}} == Democratic primary == === Candidates === *[[Eliot Spitzer]], Attorney General of New York (1999–2006) **Running mate: [[David Paterson]], New York Senate minority leader *[[Tom Suozzi]], Nassau County Executive === Campaign === On December 7, 2004, Eliot Spitzer announced his intention to seek the Democratic nomination for the 2006 election for [[Governor of New York]]. Spitzer's campaign manager was Ryan Toohey of [[Global Strategy Group]], which Spitzer had hired for his 1998 campaign for attorney general and for the gubernatorial campaign. While long rumored, Spitzer's announcement was nevertheless considered unusually early—nearly two years before the election. Some pundits believed the timing was due to Spitzer's desire to see if Senator [[Charles Schumer]], a more senior Democrat, would run. Schumer, who was largely favored in opinion polls in a hypothetical matchup against Spitzer, announced in November that he would not run for governor, instead accepting an offer to sit on the powerful [[United States Senate Committee on Finance|Finance Committee]] and head the [[Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee]]. After Schumer announced he would maintain his Senate seat, another Democrat, [[Andrew Cuomo]], announced his plans to run for Spitzer's vacated Attorney General's seat. Spitzer won an early vote of confidence on January 22, 2005, by gaining the endorsement of the [[Working Families Party]], which has taken advantage of New York's [[electoral fusion]] system to act as a kingmaker over Democratic nominees. It is backed heavily by figures from community group [[Association of Community Organizations for Reform Now|ACORN]] and [[labor unions]], particularly those that broke from the [[AFL–CIO]] to form the [[Change to Win Federation]]. In the months after the WFP endorsement, several Change to Win unions have announced that they are endorsing Spitzer under their own name, including [[UNITE HERE]], the [[Teamsters]], and the [[United Food and Commercial Workers]]. By July 2005, Spitzer had forced Governor Pataki from the race. In the latter half of 2005, Spitzer sought to further solidify support for his campaign by touring the state, seeking and giving political endorsements. These included cross endorsements with former-Bronx Borough President [[Fernando Ferrer]] in the [[New York City mayoral election, 2005|New York City Mayoral election]], [[Matthew Driscoll]] in the [[Syracuse, New York|Syracuse]] Mayoral election, and State Senator [[Byron Brown]] in the [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]] Mayoral election. The benefit to Spitzer in these endorsement deals was valuable media attention as he stumped for the candidates. As a result of Spitzer's relative speed in uniting state Democrats to his side, he had gained the respect of Democratic leaders nationwide. [[Bill Richardson (politician)|Bill Richardson]] dubbed Spitzer the "future of the Democratic Party", at a fundraiser held in June 2005 for Spitzer's gubernatorial campaign.{{citation needed|date=April 2021}} With a large polling lead in the Democratic primary,{{Cite web|url=https://www.quinnipiac.edu/x11373.xml?ReleaseID=928|title=Quinnipiac University | Polling Results|date=September 9, 2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060909075213/https://www.quinnipiac.edu/x11373.xml?ReleaseID=928|archive-date=2006-09-09}} the June 2006 [[Quinnipiac University Polling Institute]] poll showed him leading [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau]] [[county executive]] [[Tom Suozzi]] 76–13 percent, compared to a 73–13 percent lead in a May 17, 2006, poll. An additional consideration for Spitzer was the status of billionaire businessman [[Tom Golisano]], a three-time candidate on the [[Independence Party of New York|Independence Party]] ballot line. It was rumored that Golisano might run again, and that Republican Party insiders would seek to nominate him on their own party's line, thus fusing the Republican and Independence tickets for the first time in a gubernatorial election. Golisano recently switched his party affiliation to the GOP. However, on February 1, 2006, Golisano announced that he would not run for governor.[http://www.nydailynews.com/news/politics/story/387414p-328759c.html]{{dead link|date=November 2026|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} Spitzer selected [[African-American]] [[New York State Senate]] [[minority leader]] [[David Paterson]] as his choice for [[Lieutenant Governor of New York|Lieutenant Governor]] and running mate in January 2006. In New York gubernatorial elections, the most important factor in the gubernatorial candidate's choice of a lieutenant governor is the need to "balance the ticket"—that is, to widen the candidate's appeal, whether by reaching out to someone from a different geographic area, ethnic background, or has a different political base. Paterson's father [[Basil Paterson]] was also a candidate for Lt. Governor in [[1970 New York gubernatorial election|1970]]. In February 2006, Spitzer received the endorsement of then-Democrat businessman [[Donald Trump]], who had been courted by the Republicans to run against him. === Results === [[File:New York Gubernatorial Democratic primary, 2006.svg|thumb|300px|Results by county: {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#678cd7|Spitzer}} |{{legend|#8da9e2|50–60%}} |{{legend|#678cd7|60–70%}} |{{legend|#4170cd|70–80%}} |{{legend|#3358a2|80–90%}} |{{legend|#244079|90–100%}} }}]] In the Democratic primary, held on September 12, 2006, Spitzer handily defeated Suozzi, securing his party's nomination with 82% of the vote.{{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic gubernatorial primary results{{Cite web|url=https://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=89018|title=Our Campaigns - NY Governor - R Primary Race - Sep 13, 1994|website=www.ourcampaigns.com}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Eliot Spitzer]] | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 624,684 | percentage = 81.88% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Tom Suozzi]] | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 138,263 | percentage = 18.12% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 762,947 | percentage= 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==General election== ===Candidates=== *John Clifton (Libertarian) **Running mate: Donald Silberger *[[Maura DeLuca]], activist (Socialist Workers) **Running mate: Ben O'Shaughnessy *[[John Faso]], former Minority Leader of the New York Assembly (Republican and Conservative) **Running mate: C. 2006 Ohio gubernatorial election.title: 2006 Ohio gubernatorial election
2006 Ohio gubernatorial election.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2006 Ohio gubernatorial election | country = Ohio | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2002 Ohio gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2002 | next_election = 2010 Ohio gubernatorial election | next_year = 2010 | election_date = November 7, 2006 | image1 = Congressman Ted Strickland (cropped).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Ted Strickland]]''' | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | running_mate1 = '''[[Lee Fisher]]''' | popular_vote1 = '''2,435,505''' | percentage1 = '''60.54%''' | image2 = File:Ken Blackwell (12988180853) (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Ken Blackwell]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | running_mate2 = [[Tom Raga]] | popular_vote2 = 1,474,331 | percentage2 = 36.65% | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2006 Ohio gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|210px]]|County results |[[File:2006 Ohio gubernatorial election results map by congressional district.svg|210px|]]|Congressional district results |[[File:2006 Ohio gubernatorial election results map by precinct.svg|210px]]|Precinct results}} | map_caption = '''Strickland:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}}
'''Blackwell:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Bob Taft]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Ted Strickland]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | turnout = 53.25% (registered voters) {{increase}}6.07pp }} {{ElectionsOH}} The '''2006 Ohio gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006, and was a race for the [[Governor of Ohio|governor]] and [[List of lieutenant governors of Ohio|lieutenant governor of Ohio]]. Because Ohio governors are [[Term limit|limited]] to two consecutive terms in office, incumbent Governor [[Bob Taft]] was barred from running for re-election. The election was held concurrently with a [[2006 United States Senate election in Ohio|U.S. Senate election]]. The general election for governor pitted [[Ohio Secretary of State]] [[Ken Blackwell]], the Republican nominee, against [[United States Congressman]] [[Ted Strickland]] of [[Ohio's 6th congressional district]], the Democratic nominee. Their [[running mate]]s were former [[Ohio Attorney General]] [[Lee Fisher]] on the Democratic ticket and [[Ohio House of Representatives|State Representative]] [[Tom Raga]] on the Republican ticket. In the end, the contest was not close, and Strickland captured more than 60% of the vote, giving him a solid 24-point margin of victory. Strickland was declared the winner right at 7:30 P.M. EST, when the polls closed in Ohio. Blackwell called Strickland and conceded defeat at 8:45 P.M. EST.{{cite web|url=http://www.middletownjournal.com/hp/content/oh/story/news/local/2006/11/08/ddn110806gov.html |title = MiddletownJournal: Dayton, Ohio, news and information |access-date=March 25, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110512013056/http://www.middletownjournal.com/hp/content/oh/story/news/local/2006/11/08/ddn110806gov.html |archive-date=May 12, 2011 }} Strickland won most areas of the state. In particular, he trounced Blackwell in eastern Ohio, with Blackwell only carrying one county in this region (Holmes). Blackwell did well in the Cincinnati suburbs, although he only won Hamilton County, which encompasses the City of Cincinnati, by just about 2,000 votes. He did win some rural western counties as well, but Strickland defeated Blackwell in Cuyahoga County and Franklin County, home of Cleveland and Columbus respectively. Strickland also performed strongly in the [[Rust Belt]] area from Cleveland all the way to Toledo, as well as in the Akron-Youngstown Area. This would turn out to be one of the most expensive gubernatorial elections in Ohio's history. Until [[Amy Acton]] won in [[2026 Ohio gubernatorial election|2026]], this was the last time that a Democrat was elected governor of Ohio, and the only time between 1986 and 2026, as well as the first time that an [[African Americans|African American]] (Blackwell) was the major party nominee for governor of Ohio. ==Historical background== ===National attention=== As the election approached, there was increasing national attention on the Ohio gubernatorial election, focused largely on the ability of the Republican party to maintain control in Ohio. Results in Ohio in 2006 were regarded as a possible [[Bellwether (politics)|bellwether]] for the [[2008 United States presidential election|2008 presidential election]];{{cite news| url=https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=FB0E10F73F5B0C728EDDAD0894DE404482 | work=The New York Times | title=In the Race for Ohio Governor, All Sides Agree on a Need for Change | first=Ian | last=Urbina | date=April 21, 2006 | access-date=May 20, 2010}} Ohio was considered a crucial [[swing state]], with 20 [[Electoral College (United States)|electoral votes]]. Since the [[History of the United States Republican Party|Republican Party's]] inception in 1854, no Republican presidential candidate has ever been elected to office without the electoral votes of Ohio. In contrast, a Democratic candidate has won the national election without the support of Ohio eight times (1836, 1844, 1856, 1884, 1892, 1944, 1960, and 2020). Overall, Ohio's electoral votes have gone to the winner of the election 78% of the time. Comedian and talk-show host [[Jon Stewart]] taped ''[[The Daily Show]]'' from October 30 to November 2, 2006, at the Roy Bowen Theater on the campus of [[Ohio State University]]. The series of episodes was entitled "Battlefield Ohio: The Daily Show's Midwest Midterm Midtacular" and was intended to bring further national attention to the election in Ohio.[http://www.columbusdispatch.com/features-story.php?story=dispatch/2006/08/23/20060823-G1-04.html]{{dead link|date=November 2016|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}} This was only the second time that the show had been filmed in a location other than New York City. ===Ohio, Blackwell, and the 2004 election=== {{main|2004 United States election voting controversies}} Ohio played a decisive role in the [[2004 United States presidential election|2004 presidential election]], as Ohio's electoral votes would have been sufficient to swing the election from [[George W. Bush]] to [[John Kerry]] had Kerry won in Ohio. Given the importance of the state, Blackwell's role in the conduct of the election was closely scrutinized. As Ohio secretary of state, Blackwell was the state's chief elections officer. He was also an honorary co-chair for the [[George W. Bush presidential campaign, 2004|Bush re-election campaign]] in Ohio and the most prominent backer of a ballot measure to ban [[Same-sex marriage in the United States|same-sex marriage]] on the same ballot. Leading up to the election Blackwell made a number of decisions about the election process, most of which placed additional restrictions on voting. Opponents argued that Blackwell's decisions would have the effect of suppressing turnout among vulnerable populations, most of whom would be expected to vote for Kerry in the presidential contest—and that Blackwell had a conflict of interest as a co-chair of Bush's re-election campaign. Supporters argued that the Secretary of State had always been a partisan political office and that there was nothing wrong with Blackwell having a preference in the presidential elections; they denied that Blackwell's decisions were designed to benefit Bush. Reaction to Blackwell's conduct was so strong that a coalition of left-leaning organizations attempted to amend the [[Ohio Constitution]] to abolish the Secretary of State's oversight of elections, as part of a package of election reforms. The proposal was rejected by voters in November 2005.{{cite news |last1=Welsh-Huggins |first1=Andrew |title=Officials pushed out of politics |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/293108698/ |url-access=subscription |access-date=June 12, 2019 |work=Chillicothe Gazette |page=3 |agency=Associated Press |date=December 7, 2005 |quote=Blackwell opposes the legislation [to prohibit the Secretary of State from participating in a campaign other than his own], noting Ohio voters last month overwhelmingly defeated a ballot proposal that would have stripped the secretary of state of most election duties. |via=Newspapers.com}} Dissatisfaction with Blackwell's involvement in the 2004 election apparently hurt him with Ohio's African-American community; according to exit polls, Blackwell received only 20% of the African-American vote in 2006.{{cite news| url=http://www.cnn.com/ELECTION/2006//pages/results/states/OH/G/00/epolls.0.html | work=CNN | title=CNN.com – Elections 2006 | access-date=May 20, 2010}} Exit polls showed that confidence in the election process among Ohio voters was even lower than voters in Florida, the state which produced an unprecedented five-week post-election fight in 2000.{{cite news| url=http://www.cnn.com/ELECTION/2006/pages/results/states/FL/G/00/epolls.0.html | work=CNN | title=CNN.com – Elections 2006 | access-date=May 20, 2010}} However, among voters who were "very confident" that votes would be counted accurately, Blackwell actually led Strickland. ===Republican control=== Entering the 2006 campaign, Ohio had been dominated for a decade by [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]]. Republicans had held the governorship for sixteen years, occupied all statewide constitutional offices, and controlled both houses of the [[Ohio state legislature|state legislature]]. ===Important scandals=== ====Bob Taft==== {{main|Bob Taft}} At a low point in his popularity in November 2005, Taft garnered only a 6.5% approval rating.{{cite web |url=http://www.toledoblade.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID%3D%2F20051129%2FNEWS09%2F511290414 |title = toledoblade.com -- The Blade ~ Toledo Ohio |access-date=2006-04-04 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100826043024/http://www.toledoblade.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20051129%2FNEWS09%2F511290414 |archive-date=2010-08-26 }} According to polling organization Survey USA, this was a lower proportion than any governor in the United States.{{cite web|url=http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2006/50StateGov060518State.htm |title=SurveyUSA {{pipe}} America's Neighborhood Pollster |access-date=2006-07-05 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303171303/http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2006/50StateGov060518State.htm |archive-date=2016-03-03 }} A poll taken in May 2006 indicated that only 2% of Ohio residents "strongly approved" of Taft's performance. The low approval ratings led pollster [[John Zogby]] to comment, "I'm not aware of anyone who's ever sunk lower."{{cite web|url=http://www.rasmussenreports.com/2006/State%20Polls/May%202006/Ohio%20Senate%20May.htm |title = Rasmussen Reports: Election Poll 2006 - Ohio Senate |access-date=May 15, 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060526052529/http://rasmussenreports.com/2006/State%20Polls/May%202006/Ohio%20Senate%20May.htm |archive-date=May 26, 2006 }} Taft's low approval ratings follow several years of scandals. In 2005, Taft pleaded no contest to four ethics violations involving illegal gifts totaling $5,800.{{cite web |url=http://toledoblade.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID%3D%2F20060429%2FNEWS09%2F304290018 |title = toledoblade.com -- Blackwell, Petro face uphill climb |access-date=2006-04-30 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930032454/http://toledoblade.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20060429%2FNEWS09%2F304290018 |archive-date=2007-09-30 }} He was convicted of four misdemeanors and was ordered to pay a $4,000 fine and apologize to the people of Ohio. Taft is the only Ohio governor to be convicted of a crime while in office. ====Thomas Noe and Coingate==== {{main|Coingate scandal}} In 1996 the Republican controlled [[Ohio General Assembly]] removed a restriction requiring that state investments only be in safer, though lower-yielding, [[Bond (finance)|bonds]]. After the restriction was eliminated, hundreds of millions of dollars in state funds were invested by a number of investment firms with close ties to the Republican party. Among those investments was $50 million of the [[Ohio Bureau of Workers' Compensation]] fund which was given to [[Thomas Noe]], an investor in rare and unusual coins and major donor to the Republican Party including then-governor Bob Taft.{{cite web |url=http://www.columbusdispatch.com/news-story.php?story%3Ddispatch%2F2006%2F02%2F14%2F20060214-A1-00.html |title = The Columbus Dispatch - Local/State |access-date=2011-03-12 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060223012851/http://www.columbusdispatch.com/news-story.php?story=dispatch%2F2006%2F02%2F14%2F20060214-A1-00.html |archive-date=2006-02-23 }} In 2005 it was revealed that Noe could only account for $13 million of the original investment. Among the missing funds were two coins worth over $300,000 alone. Throughout 2005, there was a protracted legal battle over the release of records which Noe claimed were privileged and prosecutors claimed were in the public domain. The [[Ohio Supreme Court]] ruled 5–2 in favor of the prosecutors. On February 13, 2006, Noe was indicted on 53 counts, including: engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity (which carries a mandatory 10-year sentence), 11 counts of theft, 11 counts of money laundering, 8 counts of tampering with records, and 22 counts of forgery. The charges also accuse Noe of personally stealing $2 million. On November 20, 2006, Noe was found guilty of theft, money laundering, forgery and corrupt activity, and was sentenced to serve 18 years in prison, fined $213,000, ordered to pay the $2 million cost of his prosecution and make restitution to the Ohio Bureau of Worker's Compensation. Also in 2006, Noe pleaded guilty to three charges of using over a dozen people in 2004 as illegal "conduits" to make donations to [[George W. Bush]]'s re-election campaign of over $45,000 in order to skirt laws limiting donations in federal campaigns to $2,000. Noe was convicted and sentenced to 27 months in federal prison and ordered to pay a $136,000 fine.{{cite web |url=http://www.toledoblade.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID%3D%2F20060912%2FBREAKINGNEWS%2F60912029 |title = toledoblade.com -- Noe gets 27 months in federal prison for illegal Bush contributions |access-date=2006-09-26 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930025208/http://www.toledoblade.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20060912%2FBREAKINGNEWS%2F60912029 |archive-date=2007-09-30 }} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Bryan Flannery]], former [[Ohio House of Representatives|state representative]] and nominee for [[Ohio secretary of state]] in 2002 *[[Ted Strickland]], [[United States Congressman|U.S. representative]] ===Campaign=== When Strickland first launched his campaign, he was originally also in a tough fight for the nomination, as Columbus Mayor [[Michael B. Reflective of both the national significance of the race, as well as the powerful fundraising capabilities of both parties, Blackwell and Strickland passed the previous fundraising record set in 1998. That record, set when current Governor Bob Taft was running against Lee Fisher (Strickland's running mate), totaled a combined $18 million by the end of the election. As of September 9, 2006, Blackwell and Strickland had already raised a combined $21.2 million. Strickland led Blackwell, $11.2 million to $10 million.{{cite web |url=http://www.cantonrep.com/index.php?ID=306903&Category=13 |title=Archived copy |website=www.cantonrep.com |access-date=15 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927192419/http://www.cantonrep.com/index.php?ID=306903&Category=13 |archive-date=27 September 2007 |url-status=dead}} Most of the money raised in Ohio by both major party candidates came from a single zip code in downtown Columbus, which is home to their respective parties, labor and political groups, lobbyists and lawyers.{{Cite web |url=http://www.cleveland.com/open/plaindealer/index.ssf?%2Fbase%2Fcuyahoga%2F1150533122181290.xml&coll=2 |title=Archived copy |access-date=2011-06-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607082216/http://www.cleveland.com/open/plaindealer/index.ssf?%2Fbase%2Fcuyahoga%2F1150533122181290.xml&coll=2 |archive-date=2011-06-07 |url-status=dead }} A significant amount of money was spent by private groups on behalf of the candidates as well, the estimated combined total at the time of the May 2 primary was $50 million.{{cite news|title=Ohio again center of political stage|first=Julie Carr|last=Smyth|work=[[The Cincinnati Post]] ([[Associated Press]])|date=2006-05-04|page=A2|url=http://news.cincypost.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20060504/NEWS01/605040371|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060821161314/http://news.cincypost.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F20060504%2FNEWS01%2F605040371|archive-date=2006-08-21|quote=Spending estimates already have reached $50 million.|url-status=dead}} === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- ! '''Istook''': {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}}
'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Brad Henry]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Brad Henry]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsOK}} The '''2006 Oklahoma gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[Brad Henry]] won re-election to a second term in a landslide, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representative]] [[Ernest Istook]]. Henry took 66.5% of the vote to Istook's 33.5% and swept [[Oklahoma panhandle|all but three]] counties in the state.{{cite web |title=Governor - General Election - November 7, 2006 |url=https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/election-results/2006-election-results/2006-general-election-results/06gov.pdf |publisher=Oklahoma State Election Board |access-date=8 January 2026}} {{As of|2026}}, this remains the last time that a Democrat was elected Governor of Oklahoma, or along with the [[2006 Oklahoma state elections|concurrent elections]], won any statewide office. Republicans later swept all statewide offices on the [[2010 Oklahoma elections|2010]] ballot, and have held majorities in both state legislative chambers since the 2008 election. ==Background== Though [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] had dominated state politics for most of [[Oklahoma]]'s history, the [[Oklahoma Republican Party]] had recently gained control of the [[Oklahoma House of Representatives]] and held five of the state's six Congressional seats.Gaddie, Ronald Keith, "[http://digital.library.okstate.edu/encyclopedia/entries/R/RE030.html Oklahoma Republican Party] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903125824/http://digital.library.okstate.edu/encyclopedia/entries/R/RE030.html |date=2011-09-03 }}," ''[http://digital.library.okstate.edu/encyclopedia/ Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100531193517/http://digital.library.okstate.edu/encyclopedia/ |date=May 31, 2010 }}'' (accessed May 28, 2010). Henry's opponent, [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Ernest Istook]], was a member of the [[United States House of Representatives]], representing [[Oklahoma's 5th congressional district]]. As in many Southern states, Oklahoma has favored conservative [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] to the more liberal members of the party. Williamson]], [[Oklahoma State Senate|Oklahoma state senator]] *Jim Evanoff ===Campaign=== Istook's strongest opponent in the primary was Bob Sullivan, who positioned himself as the only "non-career politician" in the race.[[Robert J. Sullivan, Jr.]] He ran ads featuring [[Gailard Sartain]] that attacked his opponents' "career politician" background. The [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L8cnvPgcREo Sartain ads] were seen as over the top and may have hurt his chances. Sullivan said education was a top priority and had led an effort to place an initiative petition on the November 2006 ballot that would have required 65 percent of money earmarked for education be spent in the classroom.Allen, Cindy, "[http://enidnews.com/localnews/x518651839/Governor-his-challengers-debate-about-leadership-role Governor, his challengers debate about leadership role]," ''[http://enidnews.com/ Enid News & Eagle]'', June 8, 2006 (accessed May 28, 2010). ===Results=== [[File:2006OKGOVGOP.svg|thumb|300px|Results by county {{collapsible list |title=Map legend |{{legend|#D72F30|Istook—70–80%}} |{{legend|#D75D5D|Istook—60–70%}} |{{legend|#E27F7F|Istook—50–60%}} |{{legend|#FFB2B2|Istook—40–50%}} |{{legend|#FFC8CD|Istook—30–40%}} |{{legend|#DECDE6|Istook/Sullivan tie—30–40%}} |{{legend|#ffcca9|Sullivan—30–40%}} |{{legend|#ffb580|Sullivan—40–50%}} }} ]] {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican primary results{{cite web |title=Republican Primary Election - July 25, 2006 |url=https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/elections/election-results/2006-election-results/2006-primary-election-results/06reppri.pdf |publisher=Oklahoma State Election Board |access-date=8 January 2026 |pages=38-40}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Ernest Istook]] | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 99,650 | percentage = 54.71 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = [[Robert J. '''Kulongoski:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}}
'''Saxton:''' {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Ted Kulongoski]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Ted Kulongoski]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsOR}} The '''2006 Oregon gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Governor of Oregon|Governor]] [[Ted Kulongoski]] ran for a second and final term. He faced several challengers in his primary, whom he dispatched to win his party's nomination a second time, while [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominee [[Ron Saxton]], the former chair of the [[Portland Public Schools (Oregon)|Portland Public Schools Board]] and a candidate for governor in [[2002 Oregon gubernatorial election|2002]] emerged from a crowded primary. Kulongoski and Saxton were initially going to be challenged in the general election by [[Oregon State Senate|State Senator]] [[Ben Westlund]], but Westlund withdrew his candidacy before the general election. There were multiple [[independent (politician)|independent]] and [[Third party (United States)|third party]] challengers on the ballot as well. In a hard-fought campaign, Kulongoski won re-election by a surprisingly wide margin. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this marks the last occasion in which [[Columbia County, Oregon|Columbia]], [[Marion County, Oregon|Marion]], and [[Wasco County, Oregon|Wasco]] counties have voted Democratic in a gubernatorial election. ==Democratic primary== [[File:Oregon Democratic gubernatorial primary results by county, 2006.svg|thumb|Democratic primary results by county: {{collapsible list |title=Ted Kulongoski |{{legend|#7777ffff|60–65%}}{{legend|#9999ffff|55–60%}}{{legend|#afb0ffff|50–55%}}{{legend|#cdcdffff|45–50%}}{{legend|#e1e1ffff|40–45%}} }} {{collapsible list |title=Jim Hill |{{legend|#b2ffb2ff|40–45%}} }}]] ===Candidates=== * [[Jim Hill (Oregon politician)|Jim Hill]], former [[Oregon State Treasurer]], [[Oregon gubernatorial election, 2002|2002]] Democratic candidate for [[Governor of Oregon]] * [[Ted Kulongoski]], incumbent [[Governor of Oregon]] * [[Peter Sorenson]], [[Lane County, Oregon|Lane County]] Commissioner ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change| title = Democratic Primary results{{cite web |title=Official Results - 2006 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2006 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election | country = Pennsylvania | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2002 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2002 | next_election = 2010 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election | next_year = 2010 | election_date = November 7, 2006 | image_size = 150x150px | image1 = Image:Governor Rendell (169339909) (cropped).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Ed Rendell]]''' | running_mate1 = '''[[Catherine Baker Knoll]]''' | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = '''2,470,517''' | percentage1 = '''60.36%''' | image2 = Image:Lynn Swann official photo (cropped).jpg | nominee2 = [[Lynn Swann]] | running_mate2 = [[Jim Matthews (politician)|Jim Matthews]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 1,622,135 | percentage2 = 39.64% | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2006 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|260px]] |County results |[[File:2006 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election results map by congressional district.svg|260px]] |Congressional district results |[[File:PA 2006 Governor Election By Precinct.svg|260px]] |Precinct results |default=1 }} | map_size = 250px | map_caption = '''Rendell''': {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584CDE|70–80%}}{{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} {{legend0|#0D0596|>90%}}
'''Swann''': {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} {{legend0|#C21B18|80–90%}} {{legend0|#A80000|>90%}}
'''Tie''': {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Ed Rendell]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Ed Rendell]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsPA}} The '''2006 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006, and included the races for the [[governor of Pennsylvania]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Pennsylvania|lieutenant governor of Pennsylvania]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Ed Rendell]] successfully ran for re-election. Pennsylvania's first female lieutenant governor, [[Catherine Baker Knoll]], was also running for re-election. As of 2025, this is the most recent gubernatorial election in which the Democratic candidate has carried the following counties: [[Clearfield County, Pennsylvania|Clearfield]], [[Columbia County, Pennsylvania|Columbia]], [[Elk County, Pennsylvania|Elk]], [[Mercer County, Pennsylvania|Mercer]], [[Pike County, Pennsylvania|Pike,]] [[Susquehanna County, Pennsylvania|Susquehanna]], [[Warren County, Pennsylvania|Warren]], [[Wayne County, Pennsylvania|Wayne]] and [[Wyoming County, Pennsylvania|Wyoming]]. This is the last time any statewide race in Pennsylvania resulted in a candidate getting over 60% of the vote, until Governor [[Josh Shapiro]]'s re-election in [[2026 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election|2026]]. ==Background== Rendell and Knoll had the advantage of incumbency, important in the [[swing state]] of Pennsylvania. Rendell's approval rating as of May 2006 was 62%.[http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2006/50StateGov060518State.htm Survey USA] In the [[2000 United States presidential election|2000 Presidential election]], then-[[Vice President of the United States|Vice President]] [[Al Gore]] won the state 50.6%-46.4% over then-[[Texas]] [[Governor of Texas|Governor]] [[George W. Bush]]. In 2004, Senator [[John Kerry]] carried the state 50.9%-48.4% over incumbent President [[George W. Bush|Bush]]. Although the state had voted Democratic in eight of the past 12 presidential elections, its Congressional delegation had been majority Republican for years. The counties of [[Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania|Philadelphia]] and [[Allegheny County, Pennsylvania|Allegheny]] were the Democratic strongholds, while the central part of the state was where the Republican Party fared best. The 2005 statewide party registration had Democrats out-numbering Republicans in the state with 3,841,429 to 3,292,656, with 939,252 registered independent voters.[http://www.dos.state.pa.us/bcel/lib/bcel/voter_registration/2005_municipal_election_-_unofficial.pdf 2005 Municipal Election] ==Democratic primary== Michael Morrill, the [[Green Party (United States)|Green Party]]'s nominee for governor in 2002, considered challenging Rendell on a progressive liberal platform. However, on February 13, 2006, Morrill stated that he would not run, citing the toll his 2002 race had taken on his family.{{Cite web |url=http://www.morrillmajority.org/ |title=Morrill Majority |access-date=2021-06-10 |archive-date=2017-05-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510125231/http://morrillmajority.org/ |url-status=dead }}[http://www.politicspa.com/pressreleasedetailed.asp?id=1189 Morrill release] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060322063529/http://www.politicspa.com/pressreleasedetailed.asp?id=1189 and candidate for U.S. Senate in 2004 === Campaign === [[Lynn Swann]], [[Jeff Piccola]], Jim Panyard and [[William Scranton III|Bill Scranton III]] all announced their intention to run in the Republican primary for governor in 2006. Scranton, who served two terms as [[lieutenant governor of Pennsylvania]], was the son of popular former governor [[William Scranton]], and a member of the wealthy [[Scranton, Pennsylvania|Scranton family]], was the early front-runner. However, a series of blunders by his campaign,{{cite web |title=Inquirer.com: Philadelphia local news, sports, jobs, cars, homes |url=http://articles.philly.com/2006-01-27/news/25411116_1_bill-scranton-campaign-manager-first-black-governor|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151120102827/http://articles.philly.com/2006-01-27/news/25411116_1_bill-scranton-campaign-manager-first-black-governor|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 20, 2015}} and a lack of momentum from the Piccola and Panyard campaigns, moved Swann into presumptive nominee status.{{Cite web |title=Lynn Swann Goes Deep |url=https://www.si.com/vault/2006/02/27/8370760/lynn-swann-goes-deep}} The state Republican party then endorsed Swann, leading the three other candidates to drop out ahead of the March deadline to file for the primary. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title=Republican primary results}} {{Election box candidate unopposed with party link|party=Republican Party (United
