(Constitution)[http://www.hagan4gov.com/index_001.htm Hagan For Governor site] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060129012500/http://www.hagan4gov.com/index_001.htm|date=2006-01-29}} Four candidates were campaigning for governor,[http://www.politics1.com/pa.htm Politics1: Pennsylvania] but only two went on to appear on the ballot in November. Constitution candidate Hagan Smith and Independent candidate [[Russ Diamond]] were unable to secure the necessary signatures to appear on the ballot. On August 11, Green Party candidate Marakay Rogers withdrew her nominating papers, following a challenge by Pennsylvania Democrats, who alleged that more than 69,000 signatures on the petitions were fake names, unregistered voters or illegible.{{Cite web |title=Green Party candidates give up |url=http://www.dailynews.com/news/ci_4170340 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110926204547/http://www.dailynews.com/news/ci_4170340 |archive-date=2011-09-26 |access-date=2006-08-15 |website=[[Los Angeles Daily News]]}} The challenge followed a Republican drive to collect signatures to put Green candidate Carl Romanelli on [[Pennsylvania United States Senate election, 2006#Green Party candidate on the ballot|the ballot]] in the Senate race.[https://www.boston.com/news/nation/articles/2006/08/11/pa_green_party_candidates_withdraw/?rss_id=Boston.com+%2F+News+%2F+Nation Green Party candidate withdraws]{{dead link|date=May 2026|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} Rogers continued to campaign, hoping that a federal appeals court would rule favorably in a lawsuit seeking to overturn the state's signature requirement for third-party candidates.[http://www.zwire.com/site/news.cfm?newsid=15911078&BRD=2212&PAG=461&dept_id=465812&rfi=6 Minor parties sue] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930041454/http://www.zwire.com/site/news.cfm?newsid=15911078&BRD=2212&PAG=461&dept_id=465812&rfi=6|date=2007-09-30}} === Analysis === [[Image:Swann In Philly 08.25.2006.jpg|thumb|200px|right|Former [[Pittsburgh Steelers|Steeler]] [[Lynn Swann]] courts voters tailgating before a football game between Pennsylvania's two football teams, the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] and the [[Philadelphia Eagles]]{{cite news |last=Ritter |first=Kara |date=August 2006 |title=Ex-Steeler looks to sway support of Eagles' fans |work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] |url=http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_kmtpi/is_200608/ai_n16967992|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081206045542/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_kmtpi/is_200608/ai_n16967992|url-status=usurped|archive-date=December 6, 2008}}]] In July 2005, a Zogby Poll showed Rendell with only a 47% to 41% lead over Lynn Swann. Some speculated that controversy over Act 72, proposed Medicaid cuts, and possibly even a [[2005 Pennsylvania General Assembly pay raise controversy|legislative pay increase]] that was signed into law, had reduced the governor's popularity.{{cite web |last1=Sabato |first1=Larry J. |title=What Were They Thinking? |url=https://centerforpolitics.org/crystalball/ljs2006041201/ |website=Sabato's Crystal Ball |publisher=Center for Politics |access-date=30 December 2025 |date=April 12, 2006}} Rendell led in other recent polls by significantly higher margins. Following that poll, Rendell's supporters pointed out that he had raised more money than his opponents,{{Citation needed|date=March 2010}} which they felt would help him spread his message.{{Citation needed|date=March 2010}} They also pointed out that as a sitting governor, Rendell had all the traditional advantages of an incumbent.[http://www.fandm.edu/x7706.xml Madonna analysis] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051214003402/http://www.fandm.edu/x7706.xml|date=2005-12-14}}[http://www.fandm.edu/politics.xml Franklin & Marshall College] ([[Terry Madonna]]) Center for Politics & Public Affairs {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051218202657/http://www.fandm.edu/politics.xml|date=2005-12-18}} Swann hoped to perform strongly in the conservative "T" section of the state (the central and northern regions) and in his native [[western Pennsylvania]] area.{{Citation needed|date=March 2010}} [[Lynn Swann|Swann]] canvassed for votes among [[tailgate party|tailgating]] voters in [[Philadelphia]] before the [[Pittsburgh Steelers|Steelers]] game against the [[Philadelphia Eagles|Eagles]]. On February 7, Swann served as master of ceremonies for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]'s [[Super Bowl XL]] victory parade before 250,000 people.[http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/sports/steelers/s_421528.html A quarter-million thanks] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080324171425/http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/sports/steelers/s_421528.html |date=March 24, 2008 }} ''Pittsburgh Tribune-Review'' Polls in early February showed Swann and Rendell in a statistical tie.[http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/s_422413.html Rendell, Swann in dead heat] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080408042942/http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/s_422413.html|date=2008-04-08}} ''Pittsburgh Tribune-Review'' However, Swann's momentum did not survive an effective barrage of advertising from [[Ed Rendell|Rendell]] in early spring, and he had trouble keeping up with Rendell's effective fundraising.{{cite news |last1=Barnes |first1=Tom |last2=Roddy |first2=Dennis B. |date=November 8, 2006 |title=Rendell cruises to 2nd term as governor |work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |url=http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/06312/736519-178.stm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070217202953/http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/06312/736519-178.stm|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 17, 2007}} Swann's focus on reform never caught traction, possibly as a result of his vocal support for [[Chip Brightbill]] and [[Robert Jubelirer]], legislative leaders who were defeated in the May 2006 primary election.{{cite news |last=Deparle |first=Jason |date=May 18, 2006 |title=G.O.P. '''Fogarty:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Donald Carcieri]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Donald Carcieri]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | ongoing = }} {{ElectionsRI}} The '''2006 Rhode Island gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006. Incumbent Republican [[Donald Carcieri]] very narrowly defeated Democratic lieutenant governor [[Charles J. Fogarty]] in one of the closest gubernatorial elections in Rhode Island history. With a margin of 2%, this election was also the second-closest race of the [[2006 United States gubernatorial elections|2006 gubernatorial election cycle]], behind only [[2006 Minnesota gubernatorial election|the election in Minnesota]]. {{As of|2026}}, this was the last time a Republican was elected Governor of Rhode Island and the last time a Republican won any statewide office in Rhode Island. This is also the last time the Republican candidate won the counties of [[Bristol County, Rhode Island|Bristol]] and [[Washington County, Rhode Island|Washington]]. This is the last time that a gubernatorial nominee and a lieutenant gubernatorial nominee of different political parties were elected governor and lieutenant governor of Rhode Island. ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Donald Carcieri]], incumbent [[governor of Rhode Island]] ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican Party primary results{{cite web |url=http://www.elections.state.ri.us/elections/results/2006/primary/statesummary.php |title=Federal and Statewide Races Summary |publisher=Rhode Island Board of Elections |format=PDF |access-date=28 June 2018 |archive-date=28 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928133648/http://www.elections.state.ri.us/elections/results/2006/primary/statesummary.php |url-status=dead }}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Donald Carcieri (incumbent) | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 51,650 | percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 51,650 | percentage= 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Charles Fogarty]], [[List of lieutenant governors of Rhode Island|Lieutenant Governor of Rhode Island]], former [[Rhode Island State Senate|Rhode Island state senator]] ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic Party primary results{{cite web |url=http://www.elections.state.ri.us/elections/results/2006/primary/statesummary.php |title=Federal and Statewide Races Summary |publisher=Rhode Island Board of Elections |format=PDF |access-date=28 June 2018 |archive-date=28 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928133648/http://www.elections.state.ri.us/elections/results/2006/primary/statesummary.php |url-status=dead }} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Charles J. 2006 South Carolina gubernatorial electi.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2006 South Carolina gubernatorial election | country = South Carolina | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2002 South Carolina gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2002 | next_election = 2010 South Carolina gubernatorial election | next_year = 2010 | election_date = November 7, 2006 | image1 = Mark Sanford, Official Portrait, 113th Congress (cropped).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Mark Sanford]]''' | party1 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = '''601,868''' | percentage1 = '''55.12%''' | image2 = 3x4.svg | nominee2 = [[Tommy Moore (politician)|Tommy Moore]] | party2 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 489,076 | percentage2 = 44.79% | map_image = 2006 South Carolina gubernatorial election results map by county.svg | map_size = 230px | map_caption = County results
'''Sanford''': {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}}
'''Moore''': {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Mark Sanford]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Mark Sanford]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsSC}} The '''2006 South Carolina gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] [[Governor of South Carolina|Governor]] [[Mark Sanford]] won re-election against [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[South Carolina Senate|State Senator]] [[Tommy Moore (politician)|Tommy Moore]], becoming only the third Republican governor in South Carolina to win a second term ([[Robert Kingston Scott]] and [[Carroll A. Campbell Jr.]] were the others). Sanford started the campaign with a double-digit edge over Moore, and he maintained that lead to election day. During the campaign, Sanford's approval rating averaged in the mid-fifties.{{cite web |url=http://www.surveyusa.com/client/PollTrack.aspx?g=79bc576e-2f1d-4cec-a2b4-94aecce55b09 |title=Do you approve or disapprove of the job Mark Sanford is doing as Governor? |publisher=SurveyUSA}} In Sanford's re-election victory, he garnered 22% of the African American vote. ==Democratic primary== [[Tommy Moore (politician)|Tommy Moore]], a [[South Carolina Senate|state senator]] from western South Carolina, emerged with [[Florence, South Carolina|Florence]] Mayor Frank Willis as the major candidates in the Democratic [[Partisan primary|primary election]] for governor. Rumors circulated that Superintendent of Education and former [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] candidate [[Inez Tenenbaum]] might enter the race, but she ultimately chose not to run for governor nor seek re-election to her position. [[Kenneth Lamar Holland|Kenneth Holland]], a former [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representative]] from [[South Carolina's 5th congressional district|the 5th congressional district]], briefly entered the race, but dropped out a month later after failing to raise enough financial contributions. Moore and Willis traded barbs over campaign contributions made by Willis and his wife to prominent Republicans, including President [[George W. Bush]] and Senator [[Lindsey Graham]]. Attorney C. Dennis Aughtry entered the campaign at the eleventh hour and floated the idea of legalizing casinos statewide to raise money for public schools. Moore garnered more than 50% of the vote in the Democratic primary held on June 13 and thus avoided a [[Two-round system|runoff election]]. {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results{{cite web |title=South Carolina Election Returns - June 13, 2006 Democratic Primary - Official Results |url=http://www.scvotes.org/files/06primaryOfficial/DemocratStatewide.pdf |publisher=South Carolina State Election Commission |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150330064118/http://www.scvotes.org/files/06primaryOfficial/DemocratStatewide.pdf |archive-date=March 30, 2015 |url-status=dead}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Tommy Moore | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 88,092 | percentage = 63.68 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Frank Willis | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 42,317 | percentage = 30.59 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = C. Dennis Aughtry | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 7,934 | percentage = 5.74 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 138,343 | percentage = 100 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== [[File:2006 South Carolina governor Republican primary.svg|thumb|230px|Primary results by county: {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#ed8783|Sanford}} |{{legend|#ed8783|50–60%}} |{{legend|#e55651|60–70%}} |{{legend|#d02923|70–80%}} |{{legend|#b00600|80–90%}} }} {{collapsible list | title = {{legend|#c88fe4|Lovelace}} |{{legend|#c88fe4|50–60%}} |{{legend|#b368d9|60–70%}} }} ]] Portending a sign of trouble, incumbent [[Governor of South Carolina|Governor]] [[Mark Sanford]] faced a [[primary challenge]] from [[Oscar Lovelace]], a [[physician]] from the [[Midlands, South Carolina|Midlands]]. When former Governor [[David Beasley]] ran for [[South Carolina gubernatorial election, 1998|re-election in 1998]], he faced a primary challenge and went on to lose the general election to [[Jim Hodges]]. Sanford's veto of a heart center for [[Lexington County, South Carolina|Lexington County]] and theatrics such as bringing pigs to the [[South Carolina Statehouse|Statehouse]] to show his displeasure of [[pork barrel]] spending by the [[South Carolina General Assembly|General Assembly]] angered and annoyed many Republicans. However, Sanford's strategy of avoiding Lovelace and refusal to debate worked as the governor scored a decisive victory in the primary on June 13. {{Election box begin no change | title = Republican primary results{{cite web |title=South Carolina Election Returns - June 13, 2006 Republican Primary - Official Results |url=https://www.scvotes.gov/files/06primaryOfficial/RepublicanStatewide.pdf |publisher=South Carolina State Election Commission |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802021021/https://www.scvotes.gov/files/06primaryOfficial/RepublicanStatewide.pdf |archive-date=August 2, 2022 |url-status=dead}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Mark Sanford (incumbent) | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 160,238 | percentage = 64.80 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Oscar Lovelace | party = Republican Party (United States) | votes = 87,043 | percentage = 35.20 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 247,281 | percentage = 100 }} {{Election box end}} ==Campaign== Governor Mark Sanford proposed three major issues in his campaign for re-election, chief among them being the restructuring of state government. He wanted to reduce the number of statewide elected officials from nine to three and eliminate the state's Budget and Control Board. The governor insisted that these measures would reduce the number of redundant positions and make state government both more efficient and less costly. Sanford's three major issues for the campaign were: *Restructuring state government *[[School choice]] through tuition tax credits *[[Tax cuts]] and spending restraint State Senator Tommy Moore ran as a good manager of state government. He held socially conservative and fiscally moderate positions, which put him squarely at odds with the [[Libertarianism|libertarian]] incumbent. Moore disagreed with what he believed was Sanford's condescending and combative approach of dealing with the General Assembly. The senator also believed that Sanford lacked leadership skills, and that lack of leadership had brought South Carolina to a standstill over the past four years in his view. The main policy proposals that he developed were: *A rural infrastructure bank to help undeveloped counties *A governor's office that actively recruits new businesses to the state *A 30-cent tax increase on cigarettes to offset small business tax credits for employee health insurance On July 7, several weeks after the primary election, [[Lexington County, South Carolina|Lexington County]] [[South Carolina Senate|State Senator]] [[Jake Knotts]] launched a last-minute effort to place his name on the ballot as a petition candidate for governor. He had feuded with Governor Sanford over a number of issues, including the heart center for Lexington County, and supported Lovelace in the Republican primary. In order to be on the ballot in November, Knotts needed to collect 10,000 signatures of registered voters by July 17, which he failed to do. Knotts's political consultant publicly stated that he could not have raised enough money to have run a successful candidacy. There were two trains of thought on the effects of a candidacy by Knotts. It was generally believed that had Knotts entered the race, it would have split the Republican vote and helped elect Tommy Moore. However, because those who supported Knotts went on to support Moore, it was also argued that a Knotts candidacy would have in fact deprived Moore of both votes and money. === Predictions === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |- ! '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Phil Bredesen]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Phil Bredesen]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | turnout = 49.97% {{decrease}}{{Cite news |date=November 7, 2006 |title=Tennessee Voter Turnout in 2006 |work=Tennessee Secretary of State |url=https://sos.tn.gov/elections/statistics|access-date=February 28, 2023}} 0.43 [[percentage point|pp]] }} {{ElectionsTN}} The '''2006 Tennessee gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006, to elect the [[governor of Tennessee]], alongside other state and [[2006 Tennessee elections|local elections]]. [[Incumbent]] [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] Governor [[Phil Bredesen]] was re-elected to a second term with 68.6% of the vote, defeating his [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] challenger, [[Jim Bryson (politician)|Jim Bryson]]. Improving on his performance from [[2002 Tennessee gubernatorial election|2002]], Bredesen also carried every county in the state.{{Cite web |title=2006 Gubernatorial General Election Results - Tennessee |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?year=2006&fips=47&off=5&elect=0&f=0 |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=uselectionatlas.org}} As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this was the last time a Democrat won a majority of counties in the state, the last time a Democrat won any statewide race in Tennessee, and the most recent statewide election in Tennessee in which 83 of the state's 95 counties voted Democratic. Only [[Davidson County, Tennessee|Davidson]], [[Haywood County, Tennessee|Hamilton]], [[Haywood County, Tennessee|Haywood]], [[Hardeman County, Tennessee|Hardeman]], [[Houston County, Tennessee|Houston]], [[Jackson County, Tennessee|Jackson]], [[Knox County, Tennessee|Knox,]] [[Lake County, Tennessee|Lake]], [[Madison County, Tennessee|Madison,]] [[Montgomery County, Tennessee|Montgomery]], [[Rutherford County, Tennessee|Rutherford]], and [[Shelby County, Tennessee|Shelby]] counties have voted for a Democratic candidate in a presidential, senatorial, or gubernatorial race since 2006. Eight years after this, Republican governor [[Bill Haslam]] would win every county in the state when he won [[2014 Tennessee gubernatorial election|re-election]]. == Background == [[Phil Bredesen]] became governor amid a fiscal crisis, with a predicted state budget shortfall of $800 million. Much of the shortfall was due to TennCare, which was $650 million over budget.{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Gov. Phil Bredesen (D) |url=http://www.nationaljournal.com/almanac/2010/person/phil-bredesen-tn/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130216123308/http://www.nationaljournal.com/almanac/2010/person/phil-bredesen-tn/ |archive-date=2013-02-16 |work=National Journal Magazine}} Sundquist had hoped to remedy the budget shortfall by implementing an income tax, but this proved wildly unpopular and was never enacted.{{cite web |author=Roger Abramson |date=2011-01-06 |title=Phil Bredesen Made a Successful Governor for One Mind-blowing Reason: He Did Just What He Said |url=http://www.nashvillescene.com/nashville/phil-bredesen-made-a-successful-governor-for-one-mind-blowing-reason-he-did-just-what-he-said/Content?oid=2138062 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303221656/http://www.nashvillescene.com/nashville/phil-bredesen-made-a-successful-governor-for-one-mind-blowing-reason-he-did-just-what-he-said/Content?oid=2138062 |archive-date=March 3, 2016 |access-date=January 14, 2013 |work=The Nashville Scene}} Bredesen argued that services would have to be cut, saying, "you can't have Massachusetts services and Tennessee taxes." In 2003, he signed a 9% across-the-board spending cut. In 2004, he enacted a series of changes to TennCare, essentially removing 191,000 [[Medicaid]]-eligible patients and reducing benefits. By 2006, these changes had reduced the program's cost by more than $500 million. Bredesen used some of the savings to establish a "safety net" for health clinics affected by the cuts. 2006 Texas gubernatorial election.text:

'''Strayhorn:''' {{legend0|#b0ffaeff|20–30%}} {{legend0|#a8daa5ff|30–40%}} {{legend0|#8bce88ff|40–50%}} | title = [[Governor of Texas|Governor]] | before_election = [[Rick Perry]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Rick Perry]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Texas sidebar}} The '''2006 Texas gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006, to elect the [[governor of Texas]]. The election was a rare five-way race, with incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Rick Perry]] running for re-election against [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Chris Bell (politician)|Chris Bell]] and [[Independent politician|Independents]] [[Carole Keeton Strayhorn]] and [[Kinky Friedman]], as well as Libertarian nominee James Werner. Perry was re-elected to a second full term in office, winning 39% of the vote to Bell's 30%, Strayhorn's 18%, and Friedman's 12%. This was lowest percentage of the popular vote that a Texas governor had received and still won the election since [[1861 Texas gubernatorial election|1861]]. Perry carried 209 of the state's 254 counties, while Bell carried 39 and Strayhorn carried 6.{{efn|Exit polls revealed that Perry won the white vote with 46%, while Bell got 22%, Strayhorn got 16% and Friedman got 15%. Bell won 63% of African Americans, while Perry got 16%, Strayhorn got 15% and Friedman got 4%. Bell also won the Latino vote with 41%, while Perry got 31%, Strayhorn got 18% and Friedman got 4%.}} Perry was inaugurated for a second full four-year term on January 16, 2007. The ceremony was held inside the [[Texas House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] chamber at the [[Texas Capitol]] after thunderstorms canceled the planned outdoor ceremony. This remains the last time Republicans won a statewide race in Texas with only a plurality. To date, this is the most recent gubernatorial election where [[Swisher County, Texas|Swisher]], [[Crosby County, Texas|Crosby]], [[Fisher County, Texas|Fisher]], [[Haskell County, Texas|Haskell]], [[Red River County, Texas|Red River]], [[Morris County, Texas|Morris]], [[Marion County, Texas|Marion]], [[Newton County, Texas|Newton]], [[Bee County, Texas|Bee]], and [[Calhoun County, Texas|Calhoun]] counties voted for the Democratic candidate, and the most recent in which [[Cooke County, Texas|Cooke]], [[Nolan County, Texas|Nolan]], [[Wilson County, Texas|Wilson]], [[Goliad County, Texas|Goliad]], and [[Wharton County, Texas|Wharton]] counties did not vote for the Republican candidate. ==Background== Incumbent [[Rick Perry]] became governor in late 2000 when then-Governor [[George W. Bush]] resigned following his election as [[President of the United States]]. He had been elected lieutenant governor in 1998. Perry was subsequently elected governor in his own right in 2002 and was seeking a second full term in 2006. Perry's overall poll ratings had plummeted since the 2002 election, plagued by budget woes, battles over school financing reform, and a contentious and [[2003 Texas redistricting|controversial redistricting battle]]. His approval rating dropped to 38% during the latter part of the 2005 legislative session. ==Republican primary== === Candidates === * Star Locke * [[Larry Kilgore]], advocate for [[Texas secession movements|Texas secession]] * [[Rick Perry]], incumbent governor since 2000 * Rhett Smith ==== Withdrew ==== * [[Carole Keeton Strayhorn]], [[Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts|Texas Comptroller]] and former [[Railroad Commission of Texas|Railroad Commissioner]] and mayor of [[Austin, Texas|Austin]] (''withdrew December 2005, ran as independent'') ==== Declined ==== * [[Kay Bailey Hutchison]], U.S. senator since 1993 (''[[2006 United States Senate election in Texas|ran for re-election]]'') === Campaign === The race was initially expected to be a contentious three-way primary between Perry, Comptroller of Public Accounts [[Carole Keeton Strayhorn]], and U.S. senator [[Kay Bailey Hutchison]]. Hutchison declined to run for governor in late 2005, instead opting to run for re-election to the Senate. This left Strayhorn and Perry vying for the GOP nomination. Believing her chances to be better running as an independent and appealing directly to voters, rather than those of the Republican Party first, she announced her intent to challenge him in the general election instead. Had she run in the primary, the December 2005 Scripps Howard Texas Poll of match ups had Perry in the lead against Strayhorn by a 55%-24% margin. Despite weak polling numbers, Perry had the support of the Texas Republican Party. According to Perry's campaign website, he gained 142 separate endorsements. Perry had endorsements from virtually the entire Texas Republican congressional delegation (all but two members),{{Citation needed|date=March 2010}} every Republican statewide officeholder (except Strayhorn and judicial officeholders, who by law cannot endorse political candidates), 51 of the 62 members of the Texas Republican Party executive committee, and nearly every major Texas pro-business, fiscal conservative, and social conservative organization and [[political action committee|PAC]]. Perry even managed to gain the endorsement of the [[Teamsters Union]],{{Citation needed|date=March 2010}} notwithstanding Texas's strong [[right to work laws]]. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no '''Tie''': {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Jim Doyle]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jim Doyle]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | running_mate1 = '''[[Barbara Lawton]]''' | running_mate2 = [[Jean Hundertmark]] }} {{ElectionsWI}} The '''2006 Wisconsin gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2006. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Governor of Wisconsin|Governor]] [[Jim Doyle]] ran for re-election to a second term in office. He was unopposed in the Democratic primary, and faced [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. Representative]] [[Mark Andrew Green|Mark Green]], who was unopposed in the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] primary, in the general election. The campaign between Doyle and Green was competitive and hotly contested, but Doyle, whose approval ratings hovered around 50%, had the upper hand.{{Cite web | url=http://www.surveyusa.com/50State2006/50StateGovernor060921State.htm |title = SurveyUSA {{pipe}} America's Neighborhood Pollster}} In the end, Doyle defeated Green by a fairly comfortable margin, '''Hunkins:''' {{legend0|#E27F7F|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#D72F30|70–80%}}
'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[Dave Freudenthal]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Dave Freudenthal]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsWY}} The '''2006 Wyoming gubernatorial election''' took place on November 7, 2006. Incumbent Democratic Governor [[Dave Freudenthal]] won re-election in a landslide over Republican Ray Hunkins, becoming the first Democrat since [[1910 Wyoming gubernatorial election|1910]] to win every county in the state. To date, this was the last time a Democrat was elected to statewide office in Wyoming, the last time a Democrat carried every county in the state, the last gubernatorial election in which a Democrat received more than 30% of the vote, and the last statewide election in which a Democrat won any county besides [[Teton County, Wyoming|Teton]], [[Albany County, Wyoming|Albany]], [[Laramie County|Laramie]], or [[Sweetwater County, Wyoming|Sweetwater]]. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Dave Freudenthal]], incumbent [[governor of Wyoming]] *Al Hamburg, perennial candidate ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = Democratic primary results{{cite web |title=Democratic Statewide Candidates Official Summary - Wyoming Primary Election - August 22, 2006 |url=https://sos.wyo.gov/Elections/Docs/2006/06Results/D_Statewide_Candidate_Summary.pdf |publisher=Wyoming Secretary of State}} }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | candidate = Dave Freudenthal (incumbent) | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 26,550 | percentage = 89.66 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | candidate = Al Hamburg | party = Democratic Party (United States) | votes = 3,062 | percentage = 10.34 }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 29,612 | percentage= 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== *Ray Hunkins, attorney and rancher *John H.
